I have a question for the Minister of Agriculture. A news item appeared in the Financial Post recently to the effect that the agriculture committee of the United States Senate has made recommendations for the appointment of a super salesman to outsell Canadian wheat in Europe. My question is this. Is

the Canadian wheat board or any other government agency contemplating a more aggressive sales program in Europe?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROGRAM IN EUROPE
speechtext: This is a question that really should be directed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, under whose jurisdiction the Canadian wheat board comes.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):

subtopic: PROGRAM IN EUROPE
speechtext:
This question is based on an article in the Financial Post. It seems to have arisen from dissatisfaction in the United States with regard to their own selling program because, as I read the article, one European wheat importer said this:
When we buy a cargo of hard winter Canadian wheat, we can be confident that the wheat we will receive will be the grade we have ordered or better, and that the protein content will be up to specifications.
When we buy a cargo of United States wheat, we can never be sure what we will get, but we can assume that it will be at the very bottom of the permissible grade and possibly even lower.
I think it was on the basis of that statement that the Americans are becoming perhaps a little bit more active in their wheat program.

subtopic: PROGRAM IN EUROPE
speechtext: Is the government not contemplating offsetting any such program or campaign by the United States in selling wheat in Europe?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PROGRAM IN EUROPE
speechtext: It is not a question of offsetting any program. We have been competing successfully with the Americans over the years. We have men stationed in the United Kingdom and in Europe representing the wheat board who regularly visit the countries which import our wheat. The members of the Canadian wheat board themselves annually go to the United Kingdom and to the continent of Europe in order to keep in contact with the purchasers of Canadian wheat. For three years in succession I have accompanied them on those trips. A very active program is being carried on by the Canadian wheat board and the representatives of that board.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I made such a long statement at the resolution stage, and I have also answered in such great detail most of the questions asked, that I would at this time waive the opportunity of making any further remarks. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say on behalf of the official opposition that, as I indicated at the resolution stage on February 17, we stand ready to support and speed up the passage of this legislation. May I also say that realizing the mess into which this government has manoeuvred itself in respect of the scarcity of mortgage funds, we have been ready to discuss this matter since the beginning of the session. I should like to say that many of our members, from a genuine desire to speed up the passage of this legislation, have decided not to speak in this debate, and some who have spoken have curtailed their remarks substantially for the same reason. I can think of at least three occasions, and there may have been others, when the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), in inquiring from the government house leader the business of the house to be taken up next day, suggested that the housing legislation be given priority. It is a matter of record that on each of those three occasions to which I am referring, the house leader, acting on behalf of the government, turned down our suggestion.
Now, naturally the government house leader, acting as he does on behalf of the government, is perfectly within his rights in any organization as to priority of the day to day business of the house. I mention this fact merely to keep the record straight.

National Housing Act

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Order. If the hon. member will excuse me, there is still quite a bit of noise and it is difficult to hear the hon. member who has the floor.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: I have been quite disturbed by statements in this house which seem to be trying to leave the impression that the opposition are holding up this housing legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: It is a statement of fact.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
The truth of the matter is that while this house has been sitting steadily since January 14, the government has seen fit to give this important subject very little priority, juggling it around behind less important or, I should say, less urgent matters. I can use no better example of the attitude of the government and its apparent lack of interest in getting this legislation through than to refer to Hansard at page 1830. At that time the hon. member for Laurier inquired about the business to be taken up the following day, and asked the house leader whether he would give priority to this housing legislation. This was on March 7, and I do not think there can be any better example. At that time the government house leader said this:
The proposed order of business for Wednesday will be, first, the motion in the name of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to set up a joint committee on Indian affairs. Second, and related to that, we will take the second reading of Bill No. C-2, an act to amend the Indian Act. Third, we will take second reading of Bill No. C-3, an act to amend the Canada Elections Act.
The fourth order of business will be the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister dealing with the tenure of office of judges; fifth, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Public Works dealing with the National Housing Act.
Again, at the end of the discussion on March 1 the hon. member for Laurier inquired along these same lines:
May I ask if any further consideration has been given to taking the housing resolution before the matter of the Judges Act in the name of the Prime Minister.
Again the government house leader advanced his reasons for turning down this suggestion, and we find that a similar situation developed at the end of the day on February 26. At that time the hon. member for Laurier said this:
May I suggest that on Tuesday, should we complete the supplementary estimates, we might take up housing as the first item instead of the Prime Minister's resolution.
I take these few moments simply to establish the fact that we on this side of the house have tried sincerely at every opportunity that has been afforded to us to speed up this legislation. I could go on with statistics to prove the hours of debate that have been

taken up to further establish that point, but I do not think it is necessary. I do not think there can be any better examples than the ones I have cited of the lack of urgency with which the government views this very serious situation.
Frankly, lending under the National Housing Act has practically collapsed. When we think of the decreases in January and February, according to the figures given us on Friday last by the minister in terms of percentages, they are absolutely fantastic. The collapse of National Housing Act lending would not be so bad if other lending for residential construction was taking its place, but here too we find a substantial drop. We have the story in last Monday's Gazette of a 48 per cent decrease in residential construction across this country, and the reasons are obvious. There is another story in the Toronto Telegram of March 10 which carried the headline:
Mortgages Soar to H Per Cent Highest Since 1929
The article goes on to say:
Lending institutions have advised Toronto lawyers that interest rates on homes will range from 71 to 8 per cent-the highest since 1929.
Then it goes on to spell out how this is going to be handled. It says:
Lending institutions had sent out circulars advising that interest rates on houses over 25 years old, without garages, would be 8 per cent.
And so on; I am not going to take the time of the house to read it all. This is indeed a very serious situation. Like many hon. members, I have always tried to discuss housing in as non-partisan a vein as possible. However, this government is playing politics with housing, and is using it at this time as a whipping boy.
As I said at the resolution stage, the government in asking for this $500 million at this time is asking for a blank cheque to be used as it sees fit between now and the next election. If we needed further proof we got it on Friday in the minister's remarks, when he stated at page 1194 of Hansard that the total amount to be expended by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would be between $150 million and $175 million, approximately half the lending done last year, which would include direct loans to builders, if the government feels these direct loans to builders are necessary this fall. Really what the minister was saying was, direct loans to builders if necessary but not necessarily direct loans to builders. This could only mean that the government intends to squeeze out sufficient funds for builders' loans this fall from the $150 million to $175 million only if it feels that the economy needs this shot in the

arm. If that is the case, then we must conclude that a relatively small amount will be placed by C.M.H.C. through direct loans in 1960 as compared with last year.
In cutting back on housing to reduce its financial requirements the government is hoping that non-residential construction will fill the gap. If not, the government will pour in a few more millions this fall, according to the minister. This turning on and turning off of the flow of mortgage funds by the government since taking office has resulted in periods of feast and famine with respect to mortgage funds.
I should like to correct another illusion which the government has tried to create. All government spokesmen right down the line refer to the fact that this government rescued housebuilding in Canada, that nothing was being done by the former administration. This sort of propaganda is being spread from one end of the country to the other, and at this time I should like to refer to a document to which I do not think hon. members opposite will object. It is known as "Here are the Facts", and I believe additional copies are readily available to all those who are interested. I would refer hon. members to page 15, where it says:
The last years-
I emphasize the word "years".
-of the Liberal regime were characterized in the field of housing by a drastic decline in the number of new homes being built.
There could be no statement more false or misleading. The former minister of public works, now Secretary of State for External Affairs, used to indulge in this sort of nonsense but I had thought that the new minister, who was not in the opposition for 20 years, would not have followed this erroneous and misleading line. But here again the other day we had the Minister of Public Works restating this propaganda. This government, after nearly three years in office, are still trying to create the myth that nothing was being done with respect to housing before they took office.
Let us look at the facts, and I mean the real facts. In 1956, the last full year of Liberal administration and during a period of real boom when there was a real demand for funds, 135,700 homes were completed. Today the government, this self-styled saviour of the housing industry, is suggesting 125,000 starts as its objective. If the bang-up start they have made up to now is any indication, the results could well be substantially less than 100,000. So I hope this is the last time we will hear this nonsense that nothing was being done in the housing field until this government took office.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Thanks to this government the banks are doing absolutely nothing, and we had proof of that in the minister's statements on Friday. In fact when one examines the results of 1957, having in mind the administrative time lag, a great portion of the starts in 1957 were the result of Liberal policy. In 1956, the last full year of Liberal administration, 135,700 homes were completed as compared with 83,600 family formations. So I hope this is the last time we will hear attempts by government spokesmen to leave the impression that nothing was being done prior to their taking office.
Speaking in support of the legislation before us, one must consider the reasons that make these substantial increases necessary. While we do not object to these staggering increases, they do point up the degree to which the government have got themselves involved in the housing industry. They have used the taxpayers' money to bolster the economy. They have gone a step further and attempted to use these funds to regulate seasonally the flow of house construction.
Let us look at the record for a moment. In no field of government activity have government spokesmen heaped more praise upon themselves than in the field of housing. Let us see just what the government did do. When the Canadian economy began to sag late in 1957, some time after the government took office, the government poured hundreds of millions of dollars into housing in a frantic attempt to dissociate themselves from the old stigma, "Tory times are hard times" or "the

National Housing Act
party of depression", and so on. In these frantic attempts to pour money into the economy they overstimulated house building and built many of the 1959 houses in 1958.
This overstimulation had two obvious effects. First, it created a tremendous growth in housebuilding capacity which, in the face of the government's current policies, may well go unused, causing unnecessary hardship especially among the thousands of construction workers across the country. Second, the government artificially stimulated the price of land in many areas with government funds.
However, apart from the large number of housing starts resulting from the government pouring in hundreds of millions of dollars to bolster the sagging economy, the government has done relatively little in the general field of housing. The legislation before us shows no improvement in existing regulations under the National Housing Act, which would indicate to me that there is any recognition by the government of the many problems in this field at the present time and which, indeed, have existed for several years. Apparently the government are content simply to ask parliament to provide more funds, to give them a blank cheque so they may continue the policies they have been following up to this time.
Let us examine for a moment the results of these policies which the government seem to think are so satisfactory. What did these policies do for housing in 1959? Outlays on housing in Canada, which had been rising throughout 1957 and 1958, declined throughout 1959. We attempted to bring this problem to the attention of the government in the house on several occasions during the last session. The government, instead of recognizing the problem and doing something about it, contented itself with reprimanding opposition spokesmen for making such remarks. These warnings, in one case my own, were referred to in this way by the then minister of public works, as found on page 4012 of Hansard of May 26, 1959:
With regard to his earlier suggestion, I would point out to him that it does not help house building, the morale of the Canadian people or the creation of employment, to have all this calamity howling that we are getting here on this question.
That was the sort of response we got from the government last year when we attempted to point out a steadily increasing scarcity of mortgage funds. That these warnings were well founded can be proven by the dominion bureau of statistics. In their third quarter report they use these words to describe the situation in 1959:
Housing has been much affected by the availability of mortgage funds, direct lending of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was sharply reduced

early in the year, and the approved lenders finding N.H.A. loans less attractive, curtailed their lending.
Why did approved lenders, including the commercial banks, decide to curtail their lending? Simply because they could get more for their funds by buying government bonds and treasury bills. The decline in residential construction in 1959 was due to such factors as reduced direct lending by C.M.H.C., tight money conditions, and high interest rates on government bonds. Speaking of tight money conditions and high interest rates on government bonds, it seems to me there is absolutely no justification for this situation. The government, surrounded by experts, must have known when they embarked on a policy of high interest rates in 1958 that other borrowers would have to follow suit. The bond conversion of 1958, to cover the expenditures made in an attempt to partially fulfil this government's election promises, was the real beginning of our trouble with higher mortgage interest rates.
What about housing in 1960? I do not believe people are interested in what was done in 1956 or what was done in 1958, when records were set in this field. They are interested in what government policy is going to do for them in 1960. There is every indication that the demand for money will continue and that the high interest rates encouraged by the government in its own borrowings will remain unusually high, naturally adding to the cost of doing business. Its restrictive effect on house construction has been clearly shown in 1959, and the situation will be worse in 1960 unless the government fills the gap in mortgage funds.
Starts for the last five years have averaged 138,500, and this year's estimate seems to suggest 125,000. I suggest that without government support starts will fall below 100,000. Today, with some 800,000 registered at unemployment insurance offices across the country, what possible justification can there be for the government curtailing home building and not acting at once in an effort to restore confidence that the government will support a substantial program of house building in 1960, thereby enabling builders to get on with their plans? It is only by planning that the industry can keep costs at a reasonable level and at the same time organize work in a way to ensure that employees will enjoy some degree of employment security.
Surely the government will not hide its head again this year to the scarcity of mortgage funds or pursue, in a period of high unemployment, a policy of restricting house construction. Surely the government has

provided sufficient deterrent already by establishing the highest interest rates on N.H.A. housing since the act has been in effect. Now, for the first time in the history of the act, a buyer financing through N.H.A. over a 20-year period will pay more money in interest than the original purchase price of the house. Yet government spokesmen rave about what they are doing for the lower income groups in respect of housing. They continue to heap upon themselves crushing burdens of their own praise.
Well, repetition may fool some of the people, but it is not fooling the average young couple of modest means who want to own their own home. Instead, the government, by pursuing the policies of tight money and high interest rates to which I have briefly referred, are making it more difficult than ever for these people to purchase homes of their own in 1960.
Now, we have made, I think, several suggestions from this side, and it is not my intention to prolong the proceedings by reviewing them now. We have made reference to the field of urban redevelopment, and an increase from 50 per cent to 75 per cent in the federal share and of participating in the cost of sewer, water and street services to assist municipalities; to encouragement of the establishment of a secondary market for mortgages in order to facilitate the flow of more private money into mortgages, especially from the small investor; to creation of a municipal loan fund for financing major improvements; to reduction or elimination of tne insurance premiums on Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages. We do not believe there is any justification for a continuation of the present rate of the premiums.
There have been suggestions of sponsoring a national design competition so as to produce the types of houses people want. There has been a suggestion for smaller down payments. While this would lengthen the period of the mortgage, it would help to eliminate the great need for second mortgage financing which is so costly. There has been a suggestion for a dominion-provincial conference, and so on. As I mentioned, I am not going to repeat our arguments.
We have tried to indicate that the government should put its own financial house in order. We have tried to point out, and I think this is important, that with the banks now practically out of the mortgage field altogether, with the government's announced intention of cutting in half the lending they did last year, and with the lending institutions reluctant to tie up large amounts of money 79951-0-131J
National Housing Act
in long term mortgages, we believe the housing program as envisaged by this government is entirely inadequate for 1960.
However, as I said at the beginning, it is not our intention to delay the passage of the legislation. We believe the government, through its mismanagement of fiscal and monetary matters, has created an unfortunate situation which makes this legislation necessary at this time. We regret the circumstances that make it necessary for this government to ask for a blank cheque for $500 million to be used at the whim or fancy of the government between now and the next election. However, the housing requirements of many of our people remain acute. Unemployment is with us to an alarming degree. Therefore it seems to us the government should give this problem of the shortage of mortgage funds its full attention before house construction goes into a tailspin that could bring unnecessary hardship and further lack of employment to our people. We believe the urgency of this matter should transcend any political considerations, and we urge the government to get on with the job.

It is not my intention this afternoon to go into great detail in connection with the housing program. The very comprehensive statement already made by the minister indicates quite clearly that the policies and actions of the present government are so far superior to those of the previous government that there is really nothing I could add. We have only to recall that under the previous government some $100 million had been expended under this national housing program, while in the short time the present government has been in office the expenditure has risen to $1 billion.
My purpose in rising this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, is to take issue with the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland), who now realizes there is some necessity for getting on with this program. He went to great pains to try to show that the opposition had been spurring this measure along. I simply want to say that is not the case, and his remarks that the government has not tried to get this measure through are entirely inaccurate.
I would call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that on February 17, the first time this measure came before the house, it was part of the regular proceedings of that day; but on that day the opposition rose and suggested that we adjourn the regular business of the house to debate unemployment. This housing measure could very easily have been proceeded with and passed that very day if the opposition had been in any great

National Housing Act
anxiety to get on with it. I suggest to you they were not very anxious to get on with it.
Then subsequently we debated unemployment, during consideration of the supplementary estimates, for some eight or nine days. You will recall that the government was delayed in making some of its payments because there was such a great delay in passing the supplementary estimates. The opposition were not showing any great anxiety to get on with the housing program at that time.
Today they finally realize that we should get on with it, because it is a popular measure. Even so, the hon. member for Nipissing gets up and says: "We support this measure", while at the same time trying to make all sorts of criticisms about it and trying to hide their record in this field by suggesting that the government has delayed in trying to get this measure through. I am sure you will agree, sir, that that is entirely inaccurate.

Mr. Speaker, the lakehead forms an interesting microcosm in the Canadian economy. One of the reasons for this is its isolation from any large centre to the west or the east. You can take a good look at it without having extraneous factors enter into your calculations. This is what I propose to do in so far as second reading of this bill is concerned, when considering its failure to affect the lakehead situation.
I should, perhaps, begin just by noting that as of March 11 the unplaced applicants at the lakehead, or in Port Arthur, totalled over 6,000, and in Fort William they totalled approximately 4,000. The relevance of this to the housing situation becomes more apparent when you take a look at the list of occupations and discover that there are almost 380 carpenters in the twin cities who have no work at the present time. Over 1200 construction workers in those two relatively small cities are out of work. This fact indicates that there is a fundamental need at the lakehead for jobs in the construction field.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: It indicates that it is winter.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
I hear an interjection from a man who lives in the land of eternal sunshine but who seems to appreciate the fact that we have a winter problem. I might point out to the hon. member who has interjected that in the first two months of last year we had 41 housing starts in Port Arthur and Fort William as a result of the policy of the government. This year we have had exactly one housing start. If the hon. member would like to check these statistics as to the carpenters and construction workers out of work, he will

find that the incidence is higher this year than it was last year. I am obliged to put it down to the failure of the housing program of the government to generate any interest at the lakehead.
The other day the hon. member for Fort William made this point quite well when he read to the house portions of a brief from the lakehead house builders' association. This group are quite concerned over the fact that they cannot get money either to start houses on their own, let us say for speculative purposes-that is for later sale-or even find the ordinary person who can get money through the National Housing Act and wishes them to build a home. They therefore sent a letter to the hon. member for Fort William and me asking us if we would bring the problem to the attention of the minister.
I did bring this brief to the attention of the minister, and in a letter dated March 9 he gave a rather full reply. I want to put on the record-and I am sure the minister will not object-several of the paragraphs in the letter to me of March 9. In this letter the minister says:
The brief also suggests that the Bank Act be amended to permit the banks to charge an interest rate of 62 per cent per annum. Such a matter is not within my immediate jurisdiction although I am interested in it inasmuch as it affects N.H.A. loans. However a change in the bank interest rate is a matter that must be considered on the basis of its total effect on the over-all economy of the country and not purely in the light of its effect on the supply of mortgage funds.
I think I can almost paraphrase that in these words; "the supply of local mortgage funds". The letter goes on to state:
The provision of public money for mortgage lending on a large scale cannot be continued indefinitely and it is imperative that the government decrease its participation in mortgage lending as well as other expenditures in 1960. However you know that a resolution to the effect of providing more government mortgage funds has been introduced in the house. When parliament authorizes such funds, the corporation will resume its role of a residual lender.
I am sure you will appreciate that there are other centres throughout the country in a position similar to that of the lakehead in so far as availability of mortgage funds is concerned. Where loans through approved lenders are not available, the corporation will consider applications for direct loans from individual home owner applicants after parliament authorizes additional funds. The conditions under which direct loans will be made will be announced later.
It seems to me that there is in the bill a glimmer of hope beyond the rather restrictive nature of the minister's suggestion that the government hopes to limit the funds to $150 million or $175 million this year. In looking at the experience at the lakehead, which the minister says is not an isolated experience, we would trust that he will get moving on this matter as quickly as possible,

and that it there are indications that more money than $150 million or $175 million is required, he will be only too pleased to extend it.
But that does not really get at the problem of a region such as ours. When you get into the field of farming, Mr. Speaker, this government through a number of bills provides facilities, supports and subsidies to farmers in various parts of the country. We happen to be in an isolated area. We have not the kind of farm organization that can apply direct pressure, and the rebuttal I always get when the matter is brought to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture is this. "There is really nothing we can do about it; you are not on a big enough scale."
We have exactly the same situation in this housing field. Aside from the two cities of Port Arthur and Fort William there is a cluster of communities spread across northwestern Ontario in which, if the minister checks on the matter, I doubt whether in the last five years more than a dozen homes have been built with N.H.A. funds.
When the previous minister of public works took over he became very enthusiastic about a low cost house design which he passed around to all hon. members here. This house was to sell for between $5,000 and $8,000. It was going to be one of the answers of the government to looking after the people in the low income brackets. I just have not been able to find that a single one of these houses has been constructed in my particular region, a fact which indicates that somehow it has fallen short.
If you live in a town such as Geraldton with a population of 3,000, or in Hornepayne with a population of 2,000, you find there are no mortgage lending sources of any kind except the banks, and the banks will not touch loans for housing in those communities. Despite the fact that Geraldton is a fairly prosperous town, I think it has had only two houses in its history that have come from N.H.A. funds. But from statistics that are put out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and knowing that their whole program has been oriented to places of 5,000 or larger and also to places that are clustered around a metropolitan centre, if we could get the figures on just how much of the building through N.H.A. auspices has taken place in Canada I would be willing to bet that over 85 per cent of it is concentrated within 100 miles of our larger cities.
This is a failure, in so far as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are concerned, that I have pointed out previously, namely their inability to get out into the
National Housing Act
smaller places and especially into the hinterland part of the country where, as everyone knows, costs are extremely high. But it is difficult to point it out at times like this when you have a tight money situation or, as this government may prefer to call it, a tighter money situation. It seems to me that the broad, over-all policy of this government, as introduced this year under the auspices of the Minister of Finance, is becoming a noose that is strangling an area of the country such as ours.
The minister-and I am obliged to praise him for being candid-does not disguise the fact that the point that is dictating this bill and government policy at this time has nothing to do with an ideal housing policy or with a coherent government move. It is related to the consideration that the government must raise less money from other than tax sources, and must spend less money this year. At the very least this is a political position that we can recognize. I cannot admire it nor can I be for it, but at least it is clear cut. We know where this government stands. It seems to me that as far as the lakehead is concerned, it is saying to the house builders there and to the carpenters and construction workers, "You may be having it tough, but there is a greater cause for which you are suffering at the present time, namely to get this government and this country's finances into a better balance".
If you go along with this policy, that is fine. We do not happen to go along with it. We condemn it. We think it is wrong. It is more than just my personal reaction, having regard to a figure of 25 per cent of our working force unemployed. It seems to me there are very much larger issues than merely that of housing, when 25 per cent of your labour force is unemployed this early in the winter; early, that is, in the winter in statistical terms. For this reason I think we must accept this measure but we must point out, as I think the hon. member who spoke previously was trying to do, that it reflects an over-all policy that is not answering the larger needs. It is just answering the needs of the house builders or the carpenters or the construction workers.
There is one point I wanted to introduce in this debate, although I would be a silly ass to claim to know much about it. My reason for bringing it up is that I have been interested by an article written by Professor J. V. Poapst of the institute of business administration of the University of Toronto, which the hon. member for Trinity was kind enough to provide me. This article ends up by plumping for a much higher or more fluctuating rate of interest. The title of the

National Housing Act
article is "Instability in house building and its costs". On the first page of the article the writer makes this point:
The power of the government to control the rate of house building derives largely from its control over the N.H.A. mortgage market. It controls the supply of mortgage funds by making the N.H.A. interest rate attractive or unattractive to private lenders and by varying the volume of its own lending. Changes in interest rates affect the public's demand for N.H.A. mortgage loans. But changes in demand are also influenced by changes in the other terms of the loans, i.e. the maximum loan, loan to value ratio, period to maturity ratio of debt service to the loan applicant's income. Down payment requirements can also be changed by appraisal policy. Changes in the conditions and volume of N.H.A. mortgage lending (including the admission of the banks in this field in 1954) have been the preponderant cause of instability in the rate of house building in recent years.
This charge that the preponderant cause of instability in the rate of house building has been because of changes in the conditions and volume of N.H.A. mortgage lending seems to me rather serious. The minister has indicated that the money we will be getting through this bill is going to be used largely for the people in the lower income brackets, in effect for low cost housing, which is an objective we can all admire. But the question I would like to pose to the minister is this. If one of the ways to achieve this was the raise in the interest rate which was made last December to 6J per cent, why did not the minister go the whole hog and raise the interest rate much higher, and then introduce some form of subsidy to get a greater concentration on limited dividend housing or cheaper building, and so clear the way for a more stable market for people in the higher income group outside of N.H.A. altogether?
It seems to me that the government's housing policy, as a sort of offshoot of the Minister of Finance's general financial policy, is trying to ride two horses. If, as news dispatches indicate, N.H.A. mortgages are finding no takers at this particular rate and the minister is concerned, as was the previous minister, with the people with low incomes who need housing most, why did he not bifurcate his policy and free the interest rate for people who are going to buy the higher value houses, and then do something directly for the people in need whom he really wants to help?
I would judge that anything which would bring outside money into the housing picture would satisfy the house builders. It would create employment where employment is needed and is not developing at the present time, and would generally do more than the policy does at present. I have been waiting to hear a speech from the hon. member for

Trinity on this subject because he is active in this particular field. House building is his business. I hope he can go into this question of the interest rate and the effect it is having upon the stability of the house building industry in Canada at the present time.
One aspect of this bill which disappoints me is its failure to do anything about the insurance rate on mortgages under the National Housing Act. Some time ago I put a question on the order paper to try to get some perspective of the amount of money which is in the fund at the present time, and as I remember it the figure ran somewhere around $63 million. I think it was two years ago that Mr. Stewart Bates, who was appearing before a Senate committee, expressed concern over the fact that there was an increase in foreclosures, and he thought this might indicate that there were perils ahead for this fund. However, I gathef from the reassuring messages we have had from the government, even in connection with Elliot Lake, that this is not so and that the insurance fund continues to increase at a steady rate.
Following the filing of the question I received a letter from Mr. Eugene Chalifour, who I gather is a contractor living at Sillery in Quebec. He made a speech at a conference of the national house builders' association in 1959 on this very point of insuring mortgages. 1 would like to put on the record for the benefit of the minister the conclusions of this gentleman, which do spell a way out. As reported on page 6 of his address he said.
I frankly believe that every criticism of a system or any opposition of a system should be followed by a proposition.
My first is this one: why not apply the same guarantee that exists in the case of loans for housing improvements, that is 15 per cent applicable on the total of the loans? ...
Second, the creation of a mutual. Each owner who has paid insurance should be a member and would have the right to a comeback after a few years of the loan because the risk decreases as the monthly payments are made. I would recall also the equity of the debtor which is always a guarantee.
Finally, I suggest to use the reserve funds as a bank for mortgage loans.
That is the point here. At the present time we have over $63 million which could be a potential bank guarantee for mortgage loans. Mr. Chalifour goes on:
We have often talked in our conferences of a bank of mortgage loans created by Central Housing. The present fund that is already up to $63 million could no doubt be used to guarantee the billion investment by the Canadian government to help housing. This billion should remain at the disposition of the Central Housing and would be very well guaranteed by the reserve.
Recommendation should be made to the federal department so that a competent personnel in matters of insurance be hired by the Central Housing. The rate of mortgage loans should be based on the

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
risk of investment in centres more or less populated. Those who provide risky cases pay for these risks.
The mortgage insurance now in force has allowed $2,100,000,000 of loans, that is, 210,000 borrowers at $10,000 each. Why should we make these people responsible for a few 2,000 loans here and there isolated throughout the country.
These are the real risks. In other words, this gentleman has two suggestions. One is that this rate of 2 per cent is too high for insuring mortgages; second, that the fund which has already been built up could be used as a safety reserve for a continuing or revolving fund in the figure he gives of a billion dollars which would be permanently in the government's kitty as a government guarantee.
Mr. Speaker, as I said when I began my remarks, my knowledge of finance and investment is small, but I do not think this suggestion made by this gentleman is of a funny money kind or anything like that. It seems to me to have a bit of sense to it, and for that reason I would like to bring it to the minister's attention on second reading of this bill and hope that perhaps at the next session the government will consider changes in the act which will implement the two suggestions made.
I cannot end my remarks without underlining, as I have done so often in the past, the paradox or the agony of free enterprise in the house building field. The other day we had a debate on air transport, and we discovered that these free enterprisers in aviation are down asking the government to restrict things to protect their present interests, or to subsidize in one direction or another. The main purport of this brief which I have received from the lakehead house builders, and the purport of most of the recommendations in such magazines as The Canadian Builder, is to commit the government to increasing support of private industry.
There is nothing wrong with this. As a matter of fact most of my argument today has been, to a degree, in support of this; but I wish to point out and reiterate that we hear a great deal of nonsense sputtered in this country, in connection with housing, about the wonderful role of free enterprise. Again, it seems to me that in many cases free enterprise is right down there-I will not say getting their noses in the trough-trying to persuade and manipulate the government into subsidizing or supporting operations which will redound to their credit.
As a matter of fact this feeling is so strong within the house building group that it should lead us to take an even sterner or tougher look than before at just what we are doing when we vote funds to be spent in this
National Housing Act
particular field. If free enterprise is so good and so vigorous, and as wonderful as some of its proponents say it is, I cannot see why we must constantly be bailing it out with millions of dollars. I have great sympathy for the minister's aim of providing housing for those people who are among the needy of our society. I have not quite as much sympathy with regard to providing backing to these people who are shouting "free enterprise" at one moment and running around trying to pull something out of the government's treasure chest at the next.
Before concluding, I might say that I went over the speeches which were made by other hon. members at the resolution stage. I thought the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Payne) presented a very worth-while argument for the type of study and suggested action by the government in the housing field that I believe almost everyone in the house would support.
I hope the minister has taken very seriously the suggestions put forward by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, and that he will realize that they command fairly wide support in this chamber. The hon. member wants us to come to grips with the whole question of the kind of suburbs and housing developments we are getting in Canada at the present time and their effect upon the older parts of our cities, together with the services that are provided. It seems to me that such a study as the hon. member suggested would go some way toward providing answers to the questions that are bothering most of the municipalities at the present time.
In conclusion, though this may appear somewhat obvious, I wish to say that we in this group intend to vote for this measure. However, we do wish it were a better one and a more detailed one, and that it offered some indication that, sitting on the treasury benches, was one cabinet minister who did not wholly swallow the policy of the Minister of Finance but was prepared to buck it and take a broader view.

Mr. Speaker, in beginning what I have to say on this subject I should like first of all to join with all those hon. members who spoke earlier, at the resolution stage, in offering to the minister my most sincere congratulations and best wishes in the discharge of his new responsibility.
National housing is of very great importance because it provides homes for Canadian people whose incomes are small, and besides it provides employment. In addition I believe it should also give protection to the puchasers against radioactive fall-out in the event of a nuclear attack or nuclear war.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is intended to supplement and regulate the flow of mortgage funds under the National Housing Act. At the outset, may I assure the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), who is not in his seat at the moment, that if it was not for the variety of government regulations which frustrate the natural market forces, the building industry itself would not be forced to come to the government with hat in hand for what appears to be assistance but for what in reality is relief from governmental strangulation.
In order better to understand the situation in which the house building industry finds itself today it is helpful to review some of its past history. During the depression years, unfortunately, practically no new housing was built in Canada. In the war years which followed, the volume of housing construction was also very small. It is true that a few wartime housing units, were constructed but this was done quickly and some of it was on a prefabricated basis. During this same period of the depression and the war years which followed very few new apprentices were taken

into the building trades, and most of those artisans who had practised their skills in the years before were growing considerably older.
After the war there was a desperate shortage of housing. When the men and women returned home from serving in the armed forces the formation of family units was very rapid and a desperate shortage of housing accommodation developed in the immediate postwar years, reaching its peak about the late 1940's. At the same time the industry was stretched to meet this situation and had to operate in excess of its capacity. There was at the same time a desperate shortage of materials, both quantitatively and qualitatively; in addition, there was a serious shortage of skilled labour and an equally serious shortage of trained management. The situation was not without the inevitable results. There was some very poor building done in the immediate postwar years and most of the designs were those which had been used in the period preceding world war II. This is not to say that there was not some good building done. There was, but some of it, unfortunately, and I think inevitably, was below a standard which would have been expected under different circumstances.
In the ten years following world war II, some of the backlog was caught up. Year after year new supplies of building materials came into being and new building products were created and marketed; the labour force became more skilled, as those people who were engaged in the building industry throughout those years naturally acquired more competence in their various trades. In addition, management became more experienced because it had gone through some of the growing pains in this explosive expansion, and many of the mistakes which were made from time to time and from year to year were avoided in future building.
By the mid-1950's there was no longer an acute physical shortage; there were ample materials and labour to meet the effective demand in the housing industry in Canada. At the same time the situation became much more competitive. Building companies were forced by competition to improve their techniques. Many began for the first time to hire architects to prepare their plans. Others put architects on their staffs. They hired engineers to introduce into the housing industry some of those techniques which helped to cut the costs and improve the quality in other industries. At the same time, some were forced to go into the land development business in order to provide better layouts, better subdivision techniques and to reduce the cost of
National Housing Act
the ultimate housing project. The end result was a much improved product and much better value, and this process has been continuing throughout the number of years since the most critical shortage began to subside; but those improvements have been depending upon volume. Only with volume building is it possible to afford to amortize the costs of architectural services, of engineering services, to employ new labour saving devices, to engineer new building techniques, and to take advantage of the benefits of twentieth century technology. Of course, volume is dependent on financing and the building industry, I think more than any other industry in the country, is plagued by inadequate financing. It is always a feast or famine, either too much money or too little and, unfortunately, there never seems to be a long period in which there is an adequate and even flow of funds available.
The industry has struggled desperately to overcome those handicaps and to reduce the cost of its product to its customers because everybody agrees that this is how the private enterprise system works. If an industry can reduce its costs and market its products more cheaply it will increase the effective demand and thereby make a larger profit. There are three main areas of attacking the cost of the finished housing unit. They are the cost of land, the cost of money and the cost of the housing unit itself which is, at least partially tied to the availability of mortgage financing, affecting as it does the continuity of building operations. Unfortunately, government at its several levels has an overwhelming influence in each area. It is not possible to deal with each of those this afternoon, and therefore I shall content myself with dealing briefly with the third factor, namely the cost of the housing unit itself, and particularly the relationship of housing costs to a continuous supply of mortgage financing.
In the early years after the war the leading insurance companies had large blocks of funds available for investment in mortgage financing. Indeed, they invested tens of millions of dollars in national housing mortgages. They were at the time increasing their portfolios very rapidly. In later years they have been unable to meet the demands for funds and part of that, of course, is due to the fact that portfolios are now more in balance. They have increased their proportionate holdings of National Housing Act and other mortgages which they did not have during the war years and they now follow a policy designed to maintain approximately the same ratio of different types of investments.
In 1954 the National Housing Act was amended to permit the Canadian chartered

National Housing Act
banks to make insured loans under the act. This was an important addition to the supply of funds for building. More recently all sources have proved inadequate.
The government of Canada has embarked upon a policy of making direct loans through its agency, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This began under the previous administration and has continued under the present one. Under the previous administration the policy was that of a residual lender. In other words, loans were made in areas where private lending institutions did not for one reason or another wish to make mortgage loans. It also has provided loans at times when because of policy or because of the limitation of funds in any one particular fiscal period financing was not available through the normal lending sources.
The new government when it came into office changed the policy, as stated today by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland), and became the big mortgage lender. Apparently it is now to return to the policy of the former government of residual lending. Like other policies of the former government this probably looks sound when considered impartially and in the light of experience.
I have no quarrel with this belated recognition of the situation if the government takes steps to encourage a continuous flow from private sources. The money comes fundamentally from the same sources, from the same pot of resources, and just because loans are made through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation does not mean for sure that it is additional mortgage lending. Actually the government has to go into the money market and borrow funds which otherwise might, under different circumstances, have been similarly channelled into mortgage lending by the private lenders themselves.
The alarming part of the present situation is that the sum to be provided under the government's policy for 1960 is not adequate and will not do the job. The government has cut its proposed lending to half and the chartered banks are kept out of the market by government policy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: What do you mean by that last statement?
I mean simply that the Canadian chartered banks will not make mortgage loans at less than the current interest rate, which they are not permitted to do at the present time under the law.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Is the hon. member advocating an increase in the bank interest rate?
If the hon. member will contain himself until the end of my address he will know precisely what I am suggesting.
That would be something new.

As I said, the government has cut its lending to half and the banks are not in the market at present because of government policy as outlined by the minister on Friday last. There is a substantial drop in the volume of funds available from these sources without at the same time any policy to supplement the supply by other means. The present policy of the government is not adequate and will fail.
I have told the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) that he is exonerated as to everything the government has done up to the present time with respect to housing matters. He starts as of now with a clean slate. On the other hand, he will, of course, have to be held responsible for policy in the future and for the success or lack of success of whatever course the government proceeds to follow.
Or take the credit.

It is only fair in these circumstances that I should make some suggestions for his consideration. They are mine and may not necessarily reflect the view of my party. The first one is a consideration of a proposal mentioned by the hon. member for Port Arthur when he spoke a few minutes ago and which was put forward by Professor J. V. Poapst, associate professor, institute of business administration, University of Toronto, when he spoke to the Ontario regional housing conference at Ottawa on May 26, 1959. I am sure that it will be agreed that Professor Poapst has no particular axe to grind except the best interests of the Canadian people.
His proposal was that the N.H.A. interest rate be freed to seek its own level in the market. The object, of course, would be to make sure that there was some supply of N.H.A. mortgage financing available at all times. The supply would vary with the interest rate. The demand for new housing also varies as a direct function of the interest rate. But at least it would be possible to plan and the industry and private individuals who seek to provide themselves with housing accommodation would know that at all times some money would be available. This, of course, has not always been the case in the past. I should like to put on the record, if I may, just a few of the considerations raised

by Professor Poapst in his paper because I think they are well worth repeating and should form part of the record. He states:
Changes in the supply of mortgage funds in recent years have varied the fortunes of builders from feast to famine. But the effects are not limited to builders. Instability in house building must raise the cost of housing above the level which would otherwise prevail. It makes house building a tenuous field of employment. Higher wage rates are required to attract labour to the feast when there is the prospect of subsequent famine. Producers of residential building materials may be similarly affected. Also, instability discourages the development and introduction of cost reducing methods of production in the building and building materials industries where such innovations would substitute fixed for variable costs.
Further on he states:
The relative inflexibility in the N.H.A. rate has the disruptive effect of encouraging speculation over changes in the rate. This tends to create a disorderly market. If an increase in the rate is expected, private lenders tend to reduce their volume of lending, and if a decrease is expected they tend to increase it.
If approved lenders are to be induced to offer a more stable supply of N.H.A. mortgage funds, the N.H.A. rate must be more flexible. It must be free to move as other interest rates move. As I have noted already, the inadequate flexibility of the N.H.A. rate applies more to increases than to decreases. One development that would materially ease this problem would be greater acceptance by the voting public of the fact that when a lender is offered two prices for the use of his funds it is perfectly reasonable for him to prefer the higher one.
In conclusion Professor Poapst summarizes the advantages of his suggestion as follows:
1.	Higher N.H.A. rates do not mean higher financing costs for everyone. It can mean lower financing costs for borrowers who as a result of the lack of N.H.A. funds would have to turn to the conventional market and to expensive second mortgage financing.
2.	Greater flexibility in N.H.A. rates tends to reduce fluctuations in the supply of mortgage funds and thereby to reduce uncertainty over the rate of house building. This, I believe, would tend to reduce the cost of housing in the long run.
3.	More freedom for the N.H.A. rate to rise would make monetary restraint, when it is necessary, more acceptable, since the burden of restraint would be more equitably distributed. This would help to limit the seemingly non-reversible increases in prices of goods and services in general, which occur in inflationary periods.
4.	The N.H.A. mortgage market is a major component of the capital market. The net amount of N.H.A. loans approved in 1958 exceeded the gross amount of corporate bonds issued in Canadian currency during the year. The more sensitive and flexible our capital market becomes, the better it channels savings into the most desirable uses, and the stronger our national economy becomes.
I cannot possibly put the case as well as Professor Poapst has. I should like to say, however, that personally I took some considerable period of time to come to the conclusion that Professor Poapst was correct in his suggestion. As a matter of fact, I considered the matter for one full year before
National Housing Act
I came to the clear conclusion that the long term advantages to the Canadian house buying public exceeded any possible disadvantage. There is, of course, the matter of timing as to when such a policy might be put into effect. If the government was not prepared to take the risk politically of such action at a time when interest rates are going up or are very high, they could effect a change the next time the rate commenced to decline and the current N.H.A. rate is considered attractive. I think that this suggestion deserves most careful consideration by the government and its advisers.
The second consideration is to encourage the establishment of a mortgage institution along the lines suggested by Elliot N. Yarmon, president of Tankoos Yarmon Ltd., to the national house builders association convention at the Royal York hotel, Jan. 13, 1960. This is another suggestion based on experience elsewhere which has some merit and which, I think, should receive consideration by the government. I realize the minister will reply this is something in which the initiative has to be taken by private enterprise. However, I believe he and his officials could at least encourage private enterprise from the standpoint of showing interest to come forward with some concrete proposals in this connection.
Very briefly, the suggestion is to establish a private company which would issue government guaranteed certificates or debentures, the proceeds from which would be invested in N.H.A. or other mortgage investments. In order that a private company would not profit unduly at the taxpayers' expense, because of the nature of the guarantee, the return on the capital which would be required would be limited to 5 per cent; that is the same principle which is embodied in the present limited dividend section of the National Housing Act. This new non-government mortgage lending institution would make loans from coast to coast. It would be a corporate body under the same rules and regulations as now govern the construction and mortgage financing of N.H.A. housing. Its lending funds would come only from the sale to the general public of bonds fully guaranteed by the Canadian government.
The mortgage lending operations of this new body would be similar to those of conventional mortgage organizations, but its interest rate would fluctuate with local market conditions, and not be frozen at any arbitrary level as the N.H.A. level. Of course, if the N.HA.. rate were freed, this qualification of Mr. Yarmon's would not apply. The equity capital of the institution would be

National Housing Act
raised from stock subscriptions by each applicant for mortgage financing, in a fixed ratio of common stock to mortgage loans. However, because the institution would be first and foremost a body created to serve the public interest, its profits would be strictly limited to a maximum of 6 per cent. I regret the error, sir, in having previously stated it to be 5 per cent.
I would commend to the government, and to other hon. members who are interested in the subject of housing, this presentation by Mr. Yarmon. I am sure copies of it are available in full if any hon. member is interested in taking a look at it.
The third suggestion is that the government introduce amendments to the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act to permit conventional mortgage loans to a maximum of 80 per cent of the appraised value rather than 60 per cent as at present. I have taken the trouble to inquire into the experience in other countries where they have larger ratios of loan to appraised value, and the result of this survey is quite conclusive. The experience in the United Kingdom, where their building societies collect money from the public and lend it against the security of housing, is very interesting. I understand that after the war they made mortgage loans as high as 95 per cent of the appraised value, and many at 90 per cent. Even now they are making loans at 80 and 85 per cent of the appraised value. The losses resulting from this policy have been practically negligible. In the United States the experience is similar under the federal housing administration and the veterans housing administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question there? Are these conventional loans you are speaking about, through insurance companies and trust companies?

No, they are loans made, at least in Britain, under the auspices of the building societies. In the United States they are under the F.H.A. and the V.H.A. However, what I am saying is that the experience of all mortgage loans over a long period of time has been very good and leads one to the conclusion that a higher proportion of loan under the conventional system would have an equally excellent record so far as losses are concerned. The risk is practically eliminated.
The federal housing administration has made loans as high as 97 per cent of the value, and with 62.9 per cent of the total loans outstanding varying between 86 per cent and 95 per cent of the value of the house their experience has been excellent. The losses have been in a category which one

might consider to be negligible. The veterans administration advises that their experience has been similar. From the beginning of the loan guarantee program in 1945 through June, 1959 the veterans administration had guaranteed 2,672,750 loans amounting to more than $28 billion to veterans of world war II and the Korean conflict for the purchase of newly constructed homes. The average purchase price was $11,640 and the average loan was $10,505. I believe that is something over a 90 per cent loan, on the average. The conclusion that they gave me was that on these guaranteed loans their losses had amounted to less than eight cents for every $100 of the original face amount. This is such a small loss, it could be considered nominal or routine. In Canada, too, under the National Housing Act the experience has been equally favourable. Losses through default have been virtually negligible. The conclusion is that loans up to 80 per cent, could safely be made without undue risk.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: My friend is aware, is he not, that we make loans up to 90 per cent on the first $12,000 and 70 per cent of the balance up to $12,800?

Quite, but as as the minister knows what I am talking about at the present time is the proposal that the British and Canadian Insurance Companies Act be amended to permit conventional loans being made under this act up to 80 per cent of the appraised value. I have concluded that if the government were to take that action it would not involve undue risk so far as the funds of the shareholders and policy holders of these companies are concerned. The insurance companies themselves, as the minister knows, have asked that the ratio of the loan be increased to 66 per cent from its present limit of 60 per cent. I feel that this is much too conservative, if I may use that word, and merely a small step in the right direction.
Some people raise the question, what would happen in the case of a serious depression comparable to that of the 30's. My answer to that is simply that there will not be one. I feel there are a number of reasons why there will not be one, and the first is that the system today is much different from that of the 30's. Our central banking system was just established in the 30's and today it has an area of control and support for the Canadian economy which was not present in the 30's.
In addition, the variety of social welfare payments and transfer payments, including children's allowance, old age pensions, unemployment insurance et cetera are all built-in safeguards which reduce if not eliminate the possibility of any major depression. If by

any outside chance there should be a depression comparable to that in the 1930's-and I repeat that there will not be but if it did happen-
Not with a Conservative government.

My hon. friend says "not with a Conservative government". That would be the one exception I would make if he had not made it for me. But if it did happen, we would have revolution in Canada and mortgage paper would not be worth anything; and that would occur regardless of which party happened to be in power at the time.
I believe that 80 per cent loans would be perfectly safe. It is true that not all insurance companies would lend to that extent, even if they had permission to do so under the statute. But they could exercise their discretion within their own policy; and of course, in relation to the competition from other lenders, it would provide some real competition for N.H.A. loans because conventional loans would become less unacceptable alternatives to N.H.A. loans.
This provision would save Canadian home owners vast sums of money by eliminating the necessity for exhorbitant charges on second and third mortgages. There has been a recent debate in the Ontario house on the vicious nature of second and third mortgage practices in the province of Ontario. There have been references to it in this house also from time to time. My hon. friend and successor in the riding of Davenport has mentioned in this house some of his experiences with respect to second and third mortgages. Any step which this government could take which would reduce or eliminate the necessity for private individuals seeking funds from the present sources of second and third mortgages would be most welcome to all of the Canadian people. If something like this is not done, new investment organizations will, of necessity, be formed to fill the need and provide the Canadian people with this essential service.
The fourth suggestion, and the final one, is that the government should amend the National Housing Act in order to allow the Canadian chartered banks to make housing loans at the current rate. My friend, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett), will now realize that it is best for him to exercise some patience from time to time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: What does the hon. member refer to as the current rate?

The current rate is 6f per cent. I thought my hon. friend would know that.
The chartered banks made substantial loans under the National Housing Act from 1954 to
National Housing Act
date. In 1954 they made 16,906 loans; in 1955, 34,457; in 1956, 15,896; in 1957, 15,687; and in 1958, 26,135. I do not have the 1959 figure and I do not know if it is available yet. However, the five-year total from 1954 to 1958 is over 109,000 units with a total investment of over $300 million.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would just clarify his remarks there. Is he saying that he is in favour of an amendment to the Bank Act so that the banks may charge 6| per cent interest?

I made the proposal on behalf of myself that the National Housing Act be amended to permit the banks to make National Housing Act loans at the current rate. I thought my hon. friend would have understood that the first time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Is the hon. member not familiar with the terms of the Bank Act which restricts them to 6 per cent?

I am quite familiar with it; but I am sure that parliament has the authority to make an amendment to the National Housing Act which would permit the banks, notwithstanding anything contained in the Bank Act, to make loans at the current rate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That is in effect amending the Bank Act so they can charge 6J per cent.

The hon. member can make his own speech after I have finished. I hope he will do so.
It has been argued that the chartered banks are not in a position to make any substantial number of loans at the present time. That may well be the situation, but they will make some loans and each additional one would be of some assistance. Of equal importance, perhaps, the banks would have that freedom of choice which would allow them to make loans or not make loans in accordance with their individual circumstances.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
Is the hon. member in favour of allowing the chartered banks to collect more than the statutory maximum of 6 per cent?

For the third time I must repeat that in my opinion the public interest would be best served at this time by an amendment to the National Housing Act which would permit the chartered banks to make National Housing Act loans, if they are so inclined, at the current rate as set by the governor in council.

In excess of 6 per cent?

National Housing Act
For the fourth time may I say at the current rate as set by the governor in council in accordance with the National Housing Act.
No matter how high?
Amend the Bank Act.
If the government would prefer to amend the Bank Act to do the same thing, that would be their prerogative. They could present it to parliament.
The banker's friend.

There are, of course, other steps which could be taken. Time does not permit me to elaborate. The implementation of any one of the four suggestions I have put forward today would help the situation materially. The implementation of all four would help immeasurably. I urge the government to give careful consideration to these suggestions designed to stabilize the housing industry and to reduce the cost of new housing to Canadian home purchasers.

I should like to say a few words on the second reading of this bill with regard to the particular problem which we find prevalent in the rural constituencies. I speak of constituencies such as my own in which the largest town has a population of perhaps 5,000 and no more. I have several towns, of course, with a population in the range of between 3,000 and
5,000.	I would suggest, first of all, that I am completely against the suggestion put forward by the hon. member who has just spoken with regard to altering the interest rates in order to allow the bank to enter more actively into the field of housing and mortgage loans. One reason is that the banks, when they were active in this field, did not do very much in the smaller communities across this country with regard to loans for housing. I think the same comment applies to some of his other suggestions. Quite frankly, I may say I was a little bit disappointed that he did not have some better suggestion with regard to the housing situation.
I should first of all like to commend the minister on this further step in our housing policy, for with this policy has come a great deal of prosperity to my constituency. For the first time under this act we are now having some loans given to the smaller communities in western Canada. From figures in this regard it can be shown that prior to 1957 the National Housing Act was operated in the interests of large metropolitan areas and in the interests of the vested interests, the larger contractors and had little regard for the small home owners in our smaller
[Mr. Eegier.l
communities. For instance, in 1955, 14 direct loans were given out. In 1956, somewhere in the neighbourhood of 375 direct loans wert given out. In 1957 there were 2,814 direct loans as such, not including the great number of agency loans which did go out into the rural areas as well. In 1958 the figure is again over 2,000 in direct loans.
This question of direct loans through Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation is important to the people who live in the smaller communities, because this is the only type of N.H.A. loan which in many instances they have been able to get, and I would like to commend the government for their policy and especially the minister for his statement of Friday last with regard to what he intends to do this year in parliament.
We have a particular problem in our area in that the approved lenders, particularly the insurance companies, absolutely refuse to go out to the smaller towns. The reason is not that they feel these towns do not have a stable future because they have; the reason very simply is that there are not enough loans there for them to bother with. It would not even pay their overheads when there are, say, just five or six loans in each of these towns across Canada. That is the difficulty of people in our smaller towns.
As the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) suggested, the number of N.H.A. loans was practically negligible up to 1957, and then for the first time we had builders' loans under the agency system being offered to our smaller contractors in our smaller communities. This is an important development and one which I would like to see carried on. This government has done more for housing than any other government has ever done. I do not mean in just the metropolitan areas by large contractors; I am referring to what has been done for all the ordinary people across this country, which is to me the important thing. It is all very well to develop a policy whereby the big contractors get loans to build perhaps a 1,500 house subdivision, but this does not do the ordinary people any good who just want to build a new home but cannot get any mortgage funds.
This government has made it possible with its farm credit policy and' the changes in the Veterans' Land Act for the farmers and veterans to build better homes, and I would like to make a suggestion to the minister in this regard. I would suggest that he give special consideration and study to the problem of home building in our smaller communities which are now developing in western Canada. They are stable and will continue to grow, but they need help with regard to

mortgages. My suggestion would simply be that the corporation look into making a policy with regard' to issuing builders' loans, perhaps up to six at the most, to any one builder in these smaller communities.
