Mr. Speaker, one other matter before I sit down, and it is with regard to the question of housing for our senior citizens. We in Alberta have been primarily concerned with this because of the failure of the provincial government to provide adequate housing for our senior citizens. They have now embarked upon a scheme of building institutions across the province, but they are not meeting the needs of our senior citizens in that area. They have steadfastly refused to co-operate with the federal government and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation on any limited dividend scheme to provide housing for our senior citizens. I have had some experience in dealing with our older citizens, and it is my opinion that a requisite of any type of housing for our senior citizens is something to maintain the dignity and independence of these people, not to put them into an institution or a home which is later to be run by the government. They require independence and individualism, and we cannot get this by a system of institutionalized housing.

These are just a few points with regard to the question of this industry as it applies not only to my riding but I daresay to all rural ridings across the country. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this subject as it affects my area in particular. I was very surprised last year when I made an application for a branch office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to be located in my home town where considerable building is going on and was informed by the department that there have only been 13 houses built there in the last two years with loans provided by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the rest being provided by private and other sources. On making inquiries I found that these people who are borrowing money from private sources on second mortgages are in many cases paying as much as 13 per cent; and on the $2,000 or $3,000 which they borrow they pay upwards of $1,000 by way of bonus in order to get the money in the first place.
While it is true that there is no justification for moving Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation's regional office into that area because of the number of houses which were being built there, there was probably good reason to move in because so many houses were not being built under this particular act.
These houses being built are for low income people. In the main they are earning less than $5,000. Taxation statistics in 1957 indicated that 62 per cent of the wage earners in that year earned under $3,000. Under 71 per cent earned less than $3,500, and it has been pointed out that to get a $10,000 mortgage you must have an income of at least $3,500. For a mortgage of $12,000 you need a minimum income of $4,360. So it is quite obvious why the people in my area are not able to build Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation homes.
It was mentioned this afternoon that some people, and I was one, were very pleased when the government announced that they were going to build a minimum standards home for people in the low income groups. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation put out a booklet in which they outline what

National Housing Act
they expect will be in this minimum standards house, and I would like to read one sentence from the cover of this little bulletin which is as follows:
Most houses built under the N.H.A. exceed the minimum standards in a number of ways. To reduce building costs some of these features-such as bathroom, basement and electrical wiring-can be omitted without impairing the soundness of the house.
I have often wondered why in some provinces, including the province of Saskatchewan, they have a rural sanitation program where they instal bathrooms and kitchen sinks in houses. I presume the type of houses in which they are installed are the minimum standards type which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is going to build. These are not non-essentials. I would think they were essentials in a new house. If I am going to pay $10,000 to buy a house I would at least want a bathroom, and I think I would like some kind of basement as well. If not, I think I would go back and live in a wigwam.
It is quite true, as the previous speaker has pointed out, that the government and its supporters are worried about housing. The average Conservative member does not want to become too involved in the field of housing; he does not want the government to be in a position where it is controlling any of the aspects of private enterprise. We see in housing a field where private enterprise has deserted the task, left it so completely that the government was forced to put money into it, and now hon. members are complaining that the government is having to put money into it at the rate of 6 per cent.
Obviously something is being done in the high interest class, but nothing in the low interest class. If an attempt is made to get houses built under the old scheme of things the interest charged will be comparable with the interest now earned on second mortgages, which is 13 or 14 per cent plus a bonus. I hope the government will never encourage those who lend money at rates of interest such as those.
I further suggest that the government should make no attempt to encourage the construction of the house itself by leaving out such items as a bathroom and a basement. We should be able to build a fairly good house for the low income wage earners of this country, one that will serve the purpose of a fully equipped house, for between $10,000 and $12,000.
I should be happy if the government would send some of its officials into the town of New Liskeard with a view to establishing a plant there for the building of prefabricated houses. At the present time we have there a multi-million dollar woodworking plant. It

is a plant which people familiar with this business claim can build between 300 and 400 prefabricated houses per week. Once it employed a staff of 500 people, but now there is only a token staff of 20 or 30 people there. We can build prefabricated houses in New Liskeard. We have built them for Newfoundland, and demonstrated the capacities of this plant by so doing. We build a good house-a complete house-and at much less than the going cost of Central Mortgage houses.
No consideration has been given to the problem of financing as it affects people who earn low wages, particularly young married couples. Young people who have recently been married have to face a particularly expensive period of their lives, a time of their heaviest responsibilities. In most cases the husband has lately started in a job which he hopes to build up as the years go by. The needs of a growing family make it necessary to have a house with three or four bedrooms, and these people cannot just afford to buy one.
It cannot be too difficult for us to plan ahead for a few years and build houses which could be financed over a period of 50 or 60 years. The young couple could pay on this large house until their family had grown up, after which they could move out of that house, taking the equity that they have established with them, and pay for a fully paid-up small house which would suit them in their declining years. It always seems to me that we do not make plans to supply the needs of the Canadian people. We should not be too interested about maintaining the interest rates obtained by the lending institutions. They will look after themselves. But we should be very concerned about the provision of low cost housing. It seems to me that this is a field in which only the government can provide the answer and that we shall have to build once again in the class of $6,000 or $7,000 or less at a low rate of interest and with a minimum down payment.
If we do build such houses, let us economize where it is proper to do so, not by leaving out plumbing and electric wiring. It seems to me that we can solve this problem if we really try to do so and if we plan accordingly. I think we must face it today that the government will have to undertake complete responsibility for the financing in the low cost housing field. The money is not being supplied through the banks or through the lending institutions. Parliament does not seem to want to force the insurance companies to put a certain amount of their funds into low cost housing. If we do not want to do it this way, then I think that we ourselves must put more money into these things.

It is almost five o'clock, but I should like to point out that in Elliot Lake we have done all that the government hopes to do. We have built these houses, costing $15,000 or $20,000, and now we find that according to the newspapers people are locking the doors and handing in their keys. We have suggested many times that there should be disaster insurance schemes so that people living in these areas of unemployment are not forced to lose whatever money they have put into their homes; that there should be some method by which they could recuperate their losses either through insurance of this disaster type or through guarantees. I think this was one case where Central Mortgage knew something that the rest of the government did not realize, namely that there was going to be this problem in Elliot Lake. They took the opportunity of protecting themselves. I think they should have taken the opportunity, also, of protecting the people who were buying their houses. There are too many people in that area living in houses under mortgages with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation who are going to be faced with the complete loss of their equities.

The house in committee on Bill No. SD-25, for the relief of Georgette Rosenberg Korman -Mr. McCleave-Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of those instances where there are no children

Private Bills-Divorce
of the petitioner and the respondent. Consequently, it is a case with which one would have less concern than those cases where there were children involved. I say this for the reasons I have set out on other occasions. This is also an instance where private investigators were involved. As a result of their investigations they produced certain evidence which was presented. The investigators were Gerard Daigneault and Clovis Paquette.
There is a bit of difference in this particular case, which should concern this committee, as compared with others which the committee has concerned itself with previously. I only make reference to this in order to make a comparison. In other cases some of the evidence given was very scanty. Scanty questions were asked by other counsel for the petitioner, or by hon. members of the subcommittee of the other house who dealt with the question. In their very light questions they did not attempt to get too much out of the extensive information which might be available. But in this case I find that counsel for the petitioner, Mr. A. H. Lieff, Q.C., of the city of Ottawa incidentally, and hon. members of the other place also, seemed to attack this case by questioning in a more insidious manner than they had in the past. I submit this is probably the type of examination which might have gone on in one of the courts of our land if this particular case had come up in one of the provinces where it is possible to obtain a divorce through the courts, where, incidentally, these cases should be dealt with.
In this case there was extensive questioning. I make reference to it in order to draw a comparison and to express wonder as to why in this instance, compared with others, there was this desire to elicit particular information. I make reference to page 11 where Mr. Lieff, Q.C., counsel for the petitioner, asked questions of the petitioner herself. Incidentally, this was after questioning on other matters had gone on previously. But to some extent this went to the question of whether or not there was collusion, whether or not there was any arrangement, whether or not any discussions were held between the respondent and the petitioner and so on. Dispensing with the questions relating to the success of attempts at reconciliation and so on and dealing only with those questions relating to the matter of arrangements or collusion between the parties we find these questions asked by Mr. Lieff:
Q. Is there any understanding between you about it?
A. No.
Q. Did you connive at the adultery? Did you scheme about it or plan it or arrange it in any way?
A. No.
Q. Or did you have anybody arrange it for you?

A. No.
Q. Did you put any woman in his way to attempt or trap him?
A. No.
Then he goes on to deal with their relationship and it has nothing to do with the question of making any collusive arrangement. The questions are very clear. The petitioner was not merely asked, as occurs in some cases, "Did you make any arrangements", but was asked quite definitely whether she had schemed about it or planned it or arranged it or connived at it. A variety of words were used to inquire of the petitioner whether there was any possibility of collusion. Then the chairman of the committee, Senator Roebuck, asked a somewhat similar question but different to some degree:
Q. Is there any arrangement between him and you with regard to the bringing of these proceedings?
A. No, there is no arrangement.
In view of the detailed examination with respect to collusion, connivance, arrangements or making plans or agreements about bringing the case before the committee of the other place and with respect to the events leading up to the petition for divorce, one wonders, especially when the same counsel is involved in other cases, why other cases are not conducted with this desire to bring out in definite form the evidence with respect to the question of collusion or connivance. I am not saying that there was anything particularly wrong in this case. It is a rather unfortunate case and it appears that for some time marital relationships between the couple had been rather strained. From the evidence given apparently one of the parties was not desirous of pulling his full weight, as a partner in a marriage should, to try to make the marriage function properly. There was a lack of effort on the part of the respondent to provide adequately for the support of his wife.
While these things in themselves would warrant questioning whether this was the proper marital relationship that should exist and while the investigators went quite extensively into what they discovered when they visited a particular place, I submit that there is no evidence of adultery. There is evidence of conditions that one might normally expect to exist if adultery were about to take place or had taken place in the past or at that particular time but there is no evidence with respect to adultery itself. This is shown on page 13 in the questioning by Mr. Lieff of one of the investigators, Mr. Gerard Daigneault, who appeared as a witness on behalf of the petitioner. After being sworn and testifying as to his name and so on he was shown a photograph and asked to identify the person. Mr. Daigneault identified him as the

respondent and then made reference to the things he discovered. He referred to verifying certain information relating to the individual in the photograph and went on to say, as found on page 12 of the evidence:
-on September 14, 1959, accompanied by Mr. Paquette, we proceeded to 132 Fairmount avenue west, Montreal, apartment 2, at approximately 11 p.m., where, after knocking on the door a few times, the door was answered by Mr. Korman.
He makes reference to the respondent being attired in pyjamas and slippers. Then he continues:
After identifying ourselves to him we walked into the entrance, and there he wanted to talk to us in the living room which is on the righthand side. I told him that I was there on behalf of his real wife and that I wanted to see and talk to the woman who was in the bedroom.
Incidentally I might add that prior to this time there is no evidence given whether or not there was a woman in the bedroom or as to how the investigator knew there was a woman in the bedroom or anywhere else on the premises. He merely starts off by saying that on a particular day they went somewhere, knocked on the door and asked to see somebody whom they said was there.
I opened the door of the bedroom myself, and I put on the ceiling light in the bedroom myself, and in a double bed on the righthand side was the woman we had seen him with previously. At that time I went to her and asked her her name and she answered me: "Rosina di Kago''. I asked her where she was living and she said: "806 Stuart avenue, Montreal".
Q. How was she dressed?
He starts to reply and then hesitates.
A. She was kind of-I saw the top part of the pyjamas on her-
And so on. Then he says there was only one bed and it appeared to have been occupied. From the evidence given by Mr. Daigneault I would say that this is another instance where the conditions were such in the particular apartment that adultery may have taken place and could have taken place either then or before or after. But in fact there is no evidence given that adultery did take place. This is a rather keen issue in some of these cases and makes one wonder whether we are in fact asked to grant divorces on the basis of adultery or on the basis of conditions which we can easily interpret according to our own way of thinking and say that adultery may have taken place when in fact we know no such thing. We only know that certain conditions existed which under some circumstances and with a certain relationship between a man and a woman might have led to or resulted in adultery but in this particular case we know no such thing. There is not one reference to it in the evidence, except for an individual reference to the arrangements in the bedroom, and so
Private Bills-Divorce
on. There was a later reference to a studio couch having been there, which was elicited after questioning by counsel for the petitioner.
Then there is the factor of the cost of obtaining a divorce in this particular medium. I have been told, and it has been mentioned in this house, that there is a minimum- of course it can vary-cost of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $2,000 or $2,500. This amount is variously divided between legal fees, a certain amount toward expenses in connection with the activities of the investigators, a certain amount for incidental expenses and the cost of filing the petition itself in the other place which has been established, as I understand it, at $210.
There is a reference in here to the amount of income the petitioner has at the moment. There is a reference to when this couple separated. There is a reference to when they were married, which was October 23, 1955. According to an answer given on page 10 they separated at the end of July, 1959. Questions were asked of the petitioner with respect to support and income. I quote from page 10 a few questions by Mr. Lieff, counsel for the petitioner:
Q. Then, what happened? Did he leave you or did you leave him?
A. I left him.
Q. Yes. While you were living with him, did he support you?
A. No.
Q. Who did support you?
A. I supported myself.
Q. And who supported your husband?
A. I did, in the beginning.
Q. You did, in the beginning?
A. Yes.
Q. Has he supported you since the separation?
A. No.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Clerk.
Q. How much do you earn?
A. $75 a week.
Q. Did you take your husband to court to get any support from him?
A. No.
Q. Does he give you any money?
A. No.
There is a question later by the chairman, Senator Roebuck, as to the occupation of the husband and the answer is that she does not know because he has not been working since 1958. Then, Senator Bradley asks:
Q. He lived off you, in other words; is that it?
A. Yes.
Here is a couple who have been married since 1955 and the husband has not been working since 1958. The petitioner by her own evidence indicates that she supported her husband in the beginning. I would imagine that would relate to the beginning of their marriage, and this would indicate that her income had been pretty well exhausted. She was earning $75 a week. I think one is

Private Bills-Divorce
entitled to ask, where would this young lady-unless she has other means-dig up $2,000 or $2,500?
You don't know.
Of course, I do not know; if I knew I would not be asking.
Why say $2,500?
Do you know of a better figure?
What is the proper figure?
If you know it, tell me. My hon. friend knows no more about this question than he does about a lot of other questions-
Wasting time.
I would suggest if my friend wants to participate in discussing these things he should do so in the proper manner.
An insult to parliament.
An insult to the House of Commons?
That is what you are doing now.

I submit that the bringing to the House of Commons and to the other place these divorce petitions from two provinces in Canada is an insult to the House of Commons and an insult to the Senate. Insult, indeed. It is merely as a result of an invitation from the Minister of Public Works that we, in this house, are engaged in wondering, questioning and looking into them. One is entitled to wonder as to where, in circumstances like these, the money would be acquired, especially when one considers this young lady is earning $75 a week and has contributed to the support of her husband as well as supporting herself. He was not working, whether by design or circumstances, I do not know. It makes one wonder. I am not casting any reflection upon the evidence given by the petitioner herself. The evidence is there, and it is clear. She made no arrangements. She did not connive; she did not plan or scheme or arrange in any way for this divorce.
I wonder whether, without her knowledge- because the respondent is not here-through some other means, he has made arrangements. I wonder whether he has a source of income which he kept hidden from his wife during the period they were living together, or whether some arrangement was made between him and the investigators to provide the proof, not of adultery, but of circumstances under which it might reasonably be assumed adultery had taken place. I do not wish to cast any reflection upon the committee of

the other place. We know that it, too, with some 500 or 600 similar cases to deal with, has not the time to inquire as fully as they might like into all the circumstances surrounding any particular case that comes before them. I would certainly suggest that counsel for the petitioner in other cases, and hon. members of the other place on the subcommittee that deals with these matters, might use the evidence given in this particular instance as a guide for their conduct in the future, and attempt to establish these facts as they have established them in this case. There should not be any doubt left as to whether or not there is a possibility of collusion or something else with respect to the various cases.

I think one must call a halt here. All day yesterday and today we have listened to people being smeared by innuendo during these discussions, doubts cast upon people who are not here. I submit these innuendos would not be made outside of this house for fear of libel. I would suggest to you, sir, that this procedure we have been witnessing this afternoon and yesterday is an insult to the members of this house. With all due respect to you, sir, these proceedings have been highly irrelevant to the question of whether or not a divorce should be granted on the grounds upon which it is usually granted.
It is not the practice of this house to determine the question of custody of the children. We have no jurisdiction over that matter nor over the matter of maintenance. Those have never been questions for consideration in the House of Commons. I would suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that we would be far better off if we continued. If hon. members wish to discuss these things, I suggest that the members who are now criticizing attend the committee meetings and prepare themselves for them instead of raising a great number of asinine points in this chamber.

May I make some comment? I hope that you, Mr. Chairman, will allow me at least the same latitude that you allowed the hon. member for Edmonton West who was more irrelevant on this particular question than any other hon. member has been on any of these items that have yet been discussed. He makes reference to sneers and innuendos and to how this is an insult to the house. However, I am sure my hon. friend appreciates the fact that these are separate bills. This House of Commons is charged with the responsibility of dealing with them.
Oh-

I should have thought my hon. friend would have exhausted his comments while he was standing up. He will notice that I did not interrupt him. Perhaps he will extend to me the same courtesy. If he would like to make some other comments later on, I am quite sure he will have no difficulty in having the Chair recognize him.
The hon. member made reference to the procedure and suggested that this is not the proper procedure. But in no instance did he express any thought as to what should be done. I am sure he will agree with me in this. I know many of his colleagues with whom I have spoken in private will do so. I do not want to divulge their names. Then why deal with it here? Why do you not deal with the bill?

My friend the hon. member for Hamilton South will have an opportunity to make some gentle comments rather than this brash outburst we have just heard. This is the procedure that we have to deal with. I for one would welcome nothing better than to get this particular case that is before us, for instance-the situation leading up to it, the evidence and everything else -out of the hands of parliament entirely and into the place where it should properly belong, namely in the hands of the provincial jurisdiction. That is what I want to do. In this particular case we must deal with it because it is here.

speechtext: Before you call Bill No. SD-27, Mr. Chairman, may I ask what happened to Bill No. SD-26? Why are the bills not in sequence?

If the hon. member had attended the committee meetings he would have found out the reason. Some of the bills are being held up for consideration.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
In Bill No. SD-27, the 36th
report of the Senate committee, we have another case that involves investigators. I would point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that there is a great deal of similarity in the operations of these particular private investigators referred to in this case. First, I should like to ask a question of the sponsor of this bill. In looking at the preamble which states what is involved in this bill, I find at page 5 of the submission to the hon. members of the Senate of Canada in parliament assembled, the following:
The petition ... humbly showeth: . ..
5. That your petitioner ever since she discovered that the said Herman Bernard had committed the

Private Bills-Divorce
said adultery, has lived separate and apart from him, and the said Herman Bernard has not since cohabited with your petitioner.
I should like to ask the sponsor of this bill whether this is not a correct statement. If there has been some close relationship between the petitioner and Herman Bernard does that mean that this bill is not acceptable to the house?

I think the established point of law is that if, after she found out that he had been unfaithful to her, she had then had sexual relationship with him she would in effect be condoning the offence, that is to say, forgiving him or letting bygones be bygones.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: From the lawyer's point of view, would that mean that we would not be allowed to grant a divorce?
If that fact were established, a divorce should not be granted.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in this business it would be advantageous if one were a lawyer. I should like to point out that the grounds for the adultery as charged in this particular case could just as easily have been presented as having taken place between the petitioner and her husband. Let us examine what happened according to the witnesses in this case. Let us even go a little bit further back and find out how she found out that the husband was supposed to be engaged in extracurricular activities. Mr. Wright, her lawyer, as reported at page 10 of the Senate evidence, asked the following questions:
Q. Would you please tell the committee how your marriage went?
A. Well, in September when we were married, for the first month, it was quite all right. During the second month of our marriage he came home one day and told me he had to take some buyers out.
Q. Buyers?
A. Yes, for the firm, and I understand this was going on for a month or two. While he was taking out the buyers he would be coming home at 3 or 4 in the morning, and this went on for three or four times a week. I told him I did not like staying alone in the apartment by myself until 3 or 4 o'clock in the morning, and I asked: "Why does it have to be that late?" Well, he answered me very briefly. He told me it was none of my business. He has to take out the buyers and that is all there is to that. I found out that the buyers were mostly women.
Q. This is as a result-you cannot tell us what anybody else told you, but I assume this is as a result of what you were told by someone else?
A. Yes.
Then it goes on. Apparently she went to a lawyer, a Mr. Adessky, and hired him. He asked her if she would like to get some evidence and have her husband's conduct investigated, and she said she would. She gave him a photograph of her husband and told him where her husband worked. This

information was subsequently turned over to the investigators, with the information of the license plate of her husband's car and also the type of car it was.
This is what happened according to the evidence of the detectives. Mr. Peter Rosen appeared as a witness on behalf of the petitioner and having been duly sworn he testified as follows:
By the clerk of the committee:
Q. What is your name?
A. Peter Rosen.
Q. What is your age?

Q. Where do you live?
A. Montreal.
Q. What is your occupation?
A. Investigator.
By Mr. Wright:	.
Q. Mr. Rosen, I show you a photograph, being exhibit 2 in these proceedings. Have you seen that photograph before?
A. Yes, that is Mr. Herman Bernard.
Q. From whom did you receive that or who showed you this photograph?
A. I received it from Mr. Adessky, a lawyer in Montreal.
Q. Did you conduct an investigation concerning this man?
A. I did.
Q. Will you please tell the committee what investigation you made?
A. I investigated the conduct of Mr. Herman Bernard from March 13 until April 25, 1959. During that time I saw Mr. Bernard on several occasions and I found that he was seeing a certain woman that lived at 1230 Fort street.
By the Chairman (Senator Roebuck):
Q. That is of your own knowledge?
A. Yes. I followed him there, and I saw him go into the apartment on several occasions prior to April 25, 1959. I also saw Mr. Bernard with the same woman attending a movie one night during the time of investigation.
By Mr. Wright:
Q. Did you see Mr. Bernard on April 25, 1959?
A. Yes sir, I did.
Q. Will you tell the committee about this?
A. I was parked near his home at 5753 North Mount street, Montreal. He came out of his home at approximately 8 o'clock.
Q. In the evening?
A. In the evening. And he got into his car, a 1958 Chevrolet sedan, and drove down town and then went into the apartment building at 1230 Fort street. I parked my car and followed him into the apartment. He went again into apartment C -this is the third time I saw him going into that apartment. I waited around until 10 o'clock and neither Mr. Bernard nor the woman came out of the building. I taped the door of the apartment and went down to the comer and called my man. As a result of that call my man met me in front of the building.
Mr. Chairman, here is a case once more where we find, in my opinion, an invasion of the privacy of	the individual. It
turned out that this Mr. Spevack is a salesman who this investigator was able to call upon any time he wished, and it raises the question of what type of salesman he is when he is available at any time of the day or night. The evidence goes on:
Q. What was the name of your man?

A. Mr. Spevack. He met me at around 11 o'clock or shortly before 11 and we both went into the building. I rang the bell of apartment C.
Q. Had the tape been removed? You rang the bell downstairs?
A. No. We checked the tapes and found they were intact. I rang the bell, and it took a few minutes before a woman came to the door and she opened the door for us slightly.
Q. How was this woman dressed?
A. She had a bathrobe on. Before opening the door she asked who was it. I told her I had a telegram for Miss Grevatt, which was her name. It took another few seconds before the door was opened and she put her hand out to take the telegram. As that happened my man and myself pushed the door, and we were in the apartment. The woman started to yell for us to get out. I told her I wanted to see Mr. Bernard. As we were in the apartment, we pushed passed her and into a bedroom-it is a very small apartment, a living room, bedroom and kitchenette.
We have another case here of the investigators lying to get into the building, and once in there, of using rough arm tactics to push the door open after it is unlocked, to push the woman to one side, and to enter the bedroom without any justification whatsoever. Let us go on with the evidence. It continues:
Q. The same man whose picture I showed vou Exhibit 2?
A. I showed him the picture I had with me, this picture, and I asked him if this was his picture and he was Herman Bernard. He admitted it was his picture and that he was Herman Bernard.
Mr. Chairman, the Senate does not appear to be very interested in whether this method of entry was legal or illegal, or whether they used false pretences in gaining entry.

Mr. Chairman, you inquired before this point of order was raised as to what point I was making. I was examining the grounds given for this adultery charge; how the evidence was obtained, the calibre of the witnesses in this case, and how it compared with what I would imagine to be more honest evidence given in other instances. The report goes on to describe the situation.
Q. Did the bed appear to have been used by one person or more?
A. It had two pillows on it and it was pretty well disarranged.
No conclusion, obviously, could be drawn from such a statement as that. The record continues:
Q. Did you see any other clothing in the room?
A. Yes, there was men's and women's underclothing in the room.
Q. Is it possible that the woman you saw was the lady sitting next to me?
A. No, it wasn't the same woman.

Private Bills-Divorce
Here we have a case where evidence is given by two people, one of them a detective, or an investigator, whatever that really means, and the other a salesman, whatever that means in this context. They break into a house under false pretences, boldly push their way in, and by doing so they establish that they are not law abiding citizens in the common sense of the word. Then they suggest that because the man is not fully dressed and the woman is wearing a housecoat, adultery has taken place. I think it is stretching the imagination to believe that it is possible. Let me read this further passage.
By Mr. Wright:
Q. When you learned about him what did you do?
A. I started divorce proceedings, I told Mr. Adessky-
Q. When you learned about this were you living with your husband at that time?
A. Yes, and I moved out.
Q. How soon after you received this information from Mr. Adessky did you move out?
A. A few days after.
We have established that these people have been living as man and wife, yet when the woman found out she did not move out right away. She moved out a few days later. Then the lawyer, Mr. Wright, whom I have met on several occasions and who is a very sharp lawyer, asked this question:
Q. A few days after that. Between the time that you learned of it-I am sorry to have to ask you these questions-between the time you learned about this from Mr. Adessky and the time you moved out did you have any sexual relations with your husband?
A. No.
You can bet your bottom dollar that Mr. Wright is sorry he has to ask that question, but he asks it all the same. He asked it because if he had not done so the chairman of the committee of the other place would have asked it.
He did not ask these other two people if they had had a sexual relationship. All he established was that they were in a place where it could have taken place. But here we have a man and his wife and we are assuming that they did not have sexual relationship. Are we not stretching our imaginations considerably? We do not know if they had two beds in this other house where this couple were living, and I rather expect they did not. They had only been married a short time, and unless they were very well off they probably had not bought a second bed.
It would appear from page five of the submission that if this had indeed taken place there would be no divorce. I am suggesting that there were much greater grounds to prove that sexual relations had been engaged in between this man and his wife because of the fact that they live in the

same house, sleep in the same bed and have been used to having sexual relationships probably for six or seven months preceding this, than it would in the other case. It would be much more logical to expect this type of relationship to take place between these two people than it would be to say that the man had gone into a stranger's house and engaged in sexual relations. They have either done this to further the passage of this divorce or else I think we are going to find no grounds for this case. The committee can continue to hear the evidence in this case and I think it will reach the conclusion that there was an opportunity for them to engage in this relationship which would have prevented the passing of this divorce. Are we not being rather ridiculous when we say it would happen in the one case and not in the other? We only have the evidence of men who are not in the least opposed to breaking the law when it serves their own purpose-the evidence of the type of investigator who breaks into people's houses in the wee hours of the morning, give false information as to who they are, and who would steal the name plates off the door. We are taking their evidence that these conditions exist. One of them says in answer to a question:
Q. Did the bed appear to be used by one person or more?
A. The bed had two pillows on it and it was pretty well disarranged.
If this is grounds for adultery, I suggest that in this case we have certainly much more ground for considering that adultery, if you would call it adultery-

Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with the second reading of this very important bill, since its purport is to assist housing, I should like to make a

few remarks without however repeating what has already been said in this house during this debate.
I fully agree with hon. members who said that loans should be granted mostly in small rural communities and in certain outlying districts, for instance in the northern areas such as are found in the riding of Chapleau which I have the honour to represent in this house.
I am pleased to point out to the house that the C.M.H.C. has already granted loans in the main cities of my riding, especially in Amos, La Sarre, Senneterre, as well as in the mining centres of Chapais and Chibougamau.
Besides, C.M.H.C. considered loan applications from other communities like Barraute, Normetal and Macamic.
There are also other smaller rural communities which, I believe, could take advantage of this action of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
In the case of most of the small loans, the requirements concerning the rental value or resale value of these properties should not be too high.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, after listening to the many speeches made in this house on this matter, there is no doubt whatsoever that this bill is the most important that our government has introduced to relieve unemployment and to help private enterprise, more particularly in the field of construction.
I want at this time to point out a feature of particular interest to the people in my district, because it concerns direct assistance to the lumber industry.
I remember, for instance, that in 1957 when I toured my riding, I noticed almost everywhere that lumber yards were filled to capacity and that demand in this respect was uncertain and even seemed to be dropping off. However, thanks to legislation passed by this government as soon as it took over in 1957, and since then, and thanks to this bill, conditions have gradually improved to the extent where, in 1957-59, the lumber was, as we might say, disposed of almost as soon as the lumbermen could cut it.
I should like to quote just a few figures in that connection, because this afternoon I heard members take issue with the policy of the government. However, our opponents who were in the former government should be the last to take us to task for our lateness, since as you know, they were the ones who 79951-0-132

To come back to figures about housing assistance, I said earlier that the former government voted $250 million. During 195758, the present government increased the amount by $150 million, bringing it to $400 million.

Mr. Speaker, I agree that I am not an expert in the matter, but I have here a few bulletins from which I should like to read certain excerpts. In this regard, they carry weight and show quite clearly that we are going through a new era of development in the field of construction.
I have here, for instance, the bulletin of the Canadian Bank of Commerce for last

National Housing Act
October, from which I should like to quote only a few short excerpts so as not to delay any longer the passing of this measure. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall quote from the English text.
(Text) :
The heading of this bulletin of the Canadian Bank of Commerce of October was:
A New Era in Housing
I shall quote only a few remarks from this bulletin in order to save as much time as possible in the debate of this measure. Part of it reads as follows:
Outdoor barbecues, gaily coloured sports attire and all the other attributes of informal community living are part and parcel of "suburbia", a phenomenon arising out of the postwar housing boom. In many cases the houses themselves are attractively designed and well-built, set in well-planned communities that constitute small satellite towns on the border of the big city. In its neighbourliness and informality it is a reversion to the small town life of former years except that the affluence of our economy has provided us not only with more leisure, but with more ways of filling our spare time.
Sociologists are examining with interest the changes in Canadian living habits associated with the suburban housing developments and their adjuncts, the modern shopping centres, all geared to the automobile economy. In this same connection, the admirable statistics on housing issued by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which is empowered, among other things, to "encourage the development of better housing and sound community planning" are unusually revealing of social and economic change.
Further on in the bulletin I read the following:
In the years 1946-58 nearly 1,267,000 new structures and over 56,000 conversions of older structures into duplexes and apartments were completed, for a total of over 1,323,000 units. Housing starts this year are expected to be below the 165,000 made in 1958, but with a record 88,000 under construction at the first of the year, completions may be of the order of 150,000, moderately higher than last year's 147,000. This year will therefore see the completion of close to a million and a half new dwellings since the end of the war.

Mr. Speaker, I also have here a more complete review indicating the number of units which have been built since 1954. I have taken this from an article entitled "The economic picture-federal aid to housing", from which I would like to quote a few excerpts which clearly confirm that our opponents are mistaken as far as the building industry is concerned, when they say that house building will not be as prosperous this year. We find, among other things, a mention that 113,527 housing units were built in 1954; 138,276 units in 1955; 127,311 in 1956; 112,340 in 1957; 164,632 in 1958 and 141,345 in 1959.

Those figures indicate that most years have been about the same, except 1958, which was a record year, as everybody knows, and as some previous speakers have pointed out.
Since 1954, direct loans have, as you know, been granted by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and the above table shows that the number of those loans has considerably increased in the last three years. Indeed, the corporation, which, in 1954, had granted only 3,586 loans, in 1955 only 2,355 and 2,565 in 1956, awarded 25,304, 38,616 and 34,240 respectively during the last three years. Those figures are an indication of the improvement in this field since the Conservative party came into power.
Another important point concerns the change in the interest rate that can be charged by corporations that wish to lend money for housing purposes. This is what the article says in this respect:
We see that the 1954 revision gave results. Now. during the whole period, the interest rate on loans has not exceeded 6 per cent. Lately, Ottawa decided to increase the rate to 6] per cent. Is that measure likely to impede housing construction?

Most likely not. On the contrary, it should promote it. First of all, it is important to know the circumstances surrounding the introduction of that measure. Moreover, loan companies have become more reluctant with regard to loans made under N.H.A. The reason is quite simple. It is because those institutions could invest their funds at a much better rate than the 6 per cent granted by the act. It is therefore in the hope of making the act more appealing to private institutions that the government decided to increase the interest rates to 6| per cent. Banks are still limited to the 6 per cent rate, however, and for that reason must not be unduly counted on in 1960.
And the article goes on as follows, thus confirming the opinion expressed by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), when he introduced that measure to allow loan institutions to raise their interest rates to 6J per cent:
That higher interest rate will mean higher monthly payments for the borrower. However, if we consider that the repayment period, which is now 25 years, might be extended to 30 years-as it quite possibly will be-the increase in the amount of payment will not be very noticeable. The National Housing Act has often been criticized as being inadequate, in regard to lower bracket salary

workers. So far, the government of the province of Quebec had refused to extend its act for improving housing conditions to people whose loans were guaranteed by the central government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with much interest to the remarks made by the minister on February 17 and again on March 11. However, in the matter of whether or not we are doing enough toward providing housing for the people of Canada I think we should be guided by one of the old laws of economics. It would be to the effect that the government may relax, that we may begin to rest easy, if and when the price of housing begins to decline, and if and when the level of rentals begins to decline. I think the minister is going to agree immediately that we have not arrived at that position yet. The cost of housing is climbing and the level of rentals is continuing its upward spiral. We have not yet nearly reached the number of housing units that we need in the nation. It is for this reason that I hope the minister, when he concludes the debate or when he speaks in the committee stage, will answer a number of matters.
I should like to ask him why his government is asking for an allotment of $500 million if at the same time the minister announces he only intends to use $150 million as a

National Housing Act
minimum and $175 million as a maximum in the current year. I should like also to pose a question to him as to whether his proposed level of expenditure includes the revenue that is available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as a result of repayments that have been made on loans in other years. I imagine that by now this publicly owned institution is in receipt of a considerable amount of money each and every month by way of payments on loans by those who have been helped in the years gone by.
I feel it is rather odd of the government to be asking this house for authorization to spend an additional $500 million when at the same time the minister announces that it is the obvious intention of the government to limit itself to spending less than one third of the amount the house is being requested to vote. I hardly see the rationality of asking us to vote $500 million if the minister announces at the same time he does not intend to use even one third of this amount It is an odd way for the government to go about receiving legislative consent to an appropriation of public revenues.
I should like to refer for a few minutes to what the minister had to say on March 11, as reported at page 1994 of Hansard. I notice the minister refers to his intention to spend very little of this money. He says:
During the last three winters we have made loans to builders in order to give winter employment a boost. We do not know whether or not that will be done again this tall or whether it will be necessary.
Might I ask the minister and the government, do they not regard the present level of unemployment as being sufficiently urgent to make these loans available now rather than wait, as the minister has indicated he will, until spring has passed, summer has passed, and if and when we again have heavy unemployment in the winter ahead, the government may reconsider its earlier announced intention of using only a very limited amount of the money parliament is now being asked to supply. I should like to submit, very humbly, that the current level of unemployment ought to warrant the minister issuing an announcement that the loans available to builders over the past number of winters will immediately again be made available upon the passage of this legislation, in order that the exceptionally high level of unemployment might receive a measure of relief.
The minister made reference, again on March 11, to the problem of the responsibility of the municipalities vis-a-vis the responsibility of other levels of government, especially this government, in the matter of slum

clearance. The minister expressed concern lest he rob the municipalities of their sense of initiative by absolving the municipalities from paying as much as 25 per cent of the cost of slum clearance. May I once again, in all humility, assure the minister that in my opinion the municipalities in Canada-and many more than he has indicated are now participating in any slum clearance-would very much like to show a lot more initiative in this field. However, because of the not inconsequential actions of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) our municipalities are in a position where they are unable to resort to the money markets; they are unable to borrow the huge amounts of capital necessarily involved in slum clearance. I feel the government might well reconsider its position and agree to encourage the municipalities to assume the initiative in slum clearance, and to give them encouragement in a little more tangible way by reducing the municipalities' portion of the costs to somewhere in the neighbourhood of 10 per cent rather than 25 per cent.
The minister went to some length on March 11 to explain how the government of which he is a member has aided Canadians in the lower income brackets. He boasts, with some measure of justification, of the fact that the number of loans made available to those with incomes below $5,000 a year have more than doubled since the Conservatives assumed office. I should like to compliment the government in this regard. However, I should like to repeat something I expressed a number of years ago in this house. I hope this has not been done at the expense of the quality of housing that has been built. I know very well indeed that the government, when the Department of Public Works was under the auspices of the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), amended the regulations in order that the low income groups might take greater advantage of the National Housing Act. At the time this was done I voiced apprehensions and I fear that my fears have been realized in that all the government of the day did was to lower the quality of homes.
Now the government realizes that there are on the market thousands of unsold homes that are not adequate to meet the needs of the poor and yet are so high in price that if you want to buy them you might as well add another few years of mortgages on to your life and buy yourself a home that is adequate to meet the needs of your family.
The minister referred to limited dividend houses. In this regard he had this to say as reported at page 1994 of Hansard:
Of course, in this coming year or in the present year we shall have a limited amount for this purpose.

All during the minister's address in this house on March 11 I noticed his emphasis on the fact that only a very limited amount is going to be available in any of the fields of housing that we have under the National Housing Act. I would suggest to the minister that he is being a little bit unrealistic if he hopes at this time for a great increase in the projects included in the limited dividend housing field. The minister had this to say:
We trust that the good work along this line may be continued.
As long as the government is prepared to allow private enterprise to make net earnings much in excess of the allowable earnings under the limited dividend housing plan I cannot see private individuals taking much interest in making their money available to this particular housing development. They are not agreeable to limiting themselves to a 5 per cent or 6 per cent net return on their investment, even though it may be partially guaranteed, if their money is able to earn them a much higher rate in other fields of endeavour. Even the Minister of Finance announced yesterday the availability of federal government securities or bonds on the market with a yield of as high as 5.99 per cent. It is rather unrealistic to expect people, out of the goodness of their hearts, to organize limited dividend housing associations in which their equity will yield them a return of 5 per cent or 5J per cent or whatever limit the minister may prescribe if, on the other hand, they are able to ring up their broker and order bonds of the same government offering them as high as 5.99 per cent.
The minister indicated that the banks were leaving the housing field and that the investment we might expect on the part of the banks may be very little indeed. As reported at page 1997 of Hansard, in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), the minister indicated that the banks in December made 17 loans; in January, 11 loans; in February, 6 loans; and that a year ago there were 900 in December, 670 in January and 883 in February. I think all of us know why the banks are leaving the housing enterprise. They are not able to get 6| per cent that other lending institutions are able to get; and in many instances the banks can buy debentures issued by this government and obtain a yield in excess of 6 per cent. Hence why would they bother with supplying housing loans?
The minister, in reply to the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget), paid some compliment to co-operative institutions. I feel that here is one possible avenue that our government has not yet explored to anywhere near
National Housing Act
its maximum extent. There is a great deal of money that might be made available for housing in Canada if there were more active assistance to and co-operation with the whole co-operative movement of the nation. I should like to pay my respects to the people of Nova Scotia and to the people of Quebec especially for their endeavours in this regard.
Also, I feel that an appeal might be made to other provinces to look at what has been done by the provincial government of Quebec in the matter of subsidizing interest rates where necessary. I feel that this is a worthwhile endeavour for all those provincial governments that are able to afford to do this subsidizing. There are tens of thousands of families in the province of Quebec who now pay an interest rate of not more than 3 per cent simply because their own government makes to them a refund of whatever rate must be paid in excess of that rate.
I hope the minister and the government are going to give more serious consideration to the setting up of what is in effect a mortgage market. I know that there is a mortgage market. Mr. Speaker, I had not intended saying much in support of this measure to lend money to builders until I had heard some of the observations made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) and the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). The hon. member for Trinity gave in the first part of his remarks pretty well an accurate story of what had transpired at the time the National Housing Act was brought into effect. However, there are one or two details which he left out.
The situation as I remember it was that after the war was over, of course, our soldiers were demobilized and returned home. Prior to that the people of Canada had been called upon to lend their money to war savings, and to refrain from buying scarce commodities.
The demand for housing at that time was so great that it was not possible to take care of the needs of the young people who came back from overseas and to satisfy the general demand for housing. The hon. member said there was a big shortage of housing at that time. That was an understatement. Competition for material, labour and land had reached a very high level. In addition, as the hon. member stated, there was a shortage of trade skills. This was taken care of by the government starting up trade schools such as Ryerson where people were instructed in crafts until they could enter the building industry. Large scale building by enterprises other than housing began to attract both men and materials. The hydro development at Queenston to satisfy industries demand, the St. Lawrence seaway and the construction of the Toronto subway are examples.
Projects such as these made demands on materials and labour which would otherwise have gone into housing, and the total result was one of tight material supply which was very difficult to handle. It is quite right to say that the resources of the building trade were strained. Both the government and big contracting firms employed inspectors to check the work done on the sites, but it is true that many of the men who were employed did not have very much knowledge of the trade. However, an effort was made to beat the deadline and get as much work completed as is possible in the circumstances.
Another factor in increasing costs was the rapid rise in the price of land during this period of expansion. Farms on the outskirts of municipalities where land would ordinarily
National Housing Act
be selling for $1,000 an acre, cost first, $2,000, then $3,000 and, finally $10,000 or $12,000. This in itself made for great increase of costs generally. In addition, there was, of course, the shortage of materials. The Korean war came and then building contractors and factories began to stockpile again. All this was bound up with speculation and galloping inflation, with the result that the housing situation became much more serious than it would ordinarily have been.
Then industry began to expand-and to expand much more rapidly. Instead of planning for a normal increase of 4 per cent a year, provision was made for an increase of 20 per cent or 25 per cent, and material was acquired far in excess of the immediate demand. Naturally the government had to take some account of the situation and, rightly or wrongly, they were accused of creating tight money. The real aim of the government was to cut down the rate of the industrial expansion which was taking place at that time. In this, the results were not entirely successful, because industry was able to get its capital south of the border at cheaper rates from their parent organization and ended in restricting homebuilding.

All I said when I began was that I was going to fill out some necessary details left out by the hon. member for Trinity. One of the points I was dealing with was the question of supplying enough money to the industry to enable it to keep going. What occurred to me was that the builders were getting what profit there was to be made leaving the people who bought the houses to carry the burden of exorbitant

prices. When the sources of money which had been available in the past dried up, and there was no more money to be obtained from the usual lending institutions, this legislation was brought in to tap a pool of money at a reduced rate of interest which was to be guaranteed by insurance to allure or induce them to lend at 5J per cent. The loans were insured at 2 per cent, to be payable by the person who was borrowing the money. I should like to quote what the minister said on January 21, 1954, as reported at page 1316 of Hansard:
These are important provisions in that they meet the main objections often expressed to the banks being in the mortgage business. The insurance protects the banks and other lenders against substantial losses on their mortgage account and there are provisions for liquidity and marketability.
At the particular time that I raised the matter I did not think it was a fair deal to the person who was borrowing the money, that he should have to pay the premium for somebody else's protection. If you want to protect your car, your home or anything you value to protect you against loss you gladly pay the premium for that protection; but here you have the case of an individual borrowing money from a lender and he is being asked to pay a premium not to give him protection but to protect the lender. I do not think it was fair to load this extra burden. I think there should be equity redemption insurance for the same premium as the lender paid. The man who is borrowing the money should have had some protection in so far as his property is concerned in case something happened to him. I thought he should have the same protection as the lender, and at the time I was told that I was radical and that I was talking along the socialist lines, which I deny. I could not agree to it then and I cannot agree to it now. Now they have raised the interest rates and the insurance protection should be withdrawn. In the olden days they used to call it usury and now they call it interest.

I intend to take only a few minutes, Mr. Speaker. There are one or two questions I have to raise in regard to the necessity of further Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation funds to support housing development in the Yukon. Until recently there was no housing development at all in the Yukon under the National Housing Act. The down payment which had to be raised in order to commence building with only the loan that was provided under the National Housing Act was too large an amount to raise.
Early in January of 1958, when I first arrived to take my seat here, I obtained the concurrence of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) and the then minister of public works (Mr. Green) to the implementation of a low rental housing scheme in Whitehorse, a scheme which was to be confined to Whitehorse but which, if the need was displayed, could have been implemented in other communities in the Yukon. This was the first time that such a proposal had been made and it almost achieved success.
Under such a scheme, of course, it was necessary for the three levels of government to co-operate, that is, the federal, the territorial and the municipal.
Housing accommodation throughout the Yukon is a matter of deep concern to all government bodies, much of it being substandard and detrimental to the health and welfare of Yukon residents and the occupants of such housing while at the same time providing a very meagre tax base for the raising of revenue in the municipalities concerned. Such conditions, as Commissioner Collins of the Yukon pointed out on one occasion, invariably accompanied the march of settlement across Canada, except where measures of aid have been made available by company or other assisted programs. In the Yukon several factors impose hardship on families of low and moderate incomes. I am quoting Commissioner Collins:
I believe the first to be the non-availability of reasonable accommodation for purchase or rental within their means, consideration being given to the cost of services, heating and other living expenses. The second is the seasonal character of much of the employment which fails to provide the necessary annual income. The third is the impermanency of the economy which does not encourage an attitude of fixed residence or the desire to become financially involved in the future of events. Outside the larger settlements other adverse factors come into play such as those which inhibit agricultural pursuits or other and normal forms of self-employment.

On this occasion the commissioner of the Yukon lay before the council a low rental housing scheme, a scheme which, as I have already said, was approved in principle by the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the then minister of public works as well as the minister of northern affairs and national resources. It was arranged that detailed plans would be completed and the necessary drafts of the agreements to be entered into between the federal government and the territorial government would be prepared and it was just about at that time the twenty third parliament come to an end.
It was on February 10, 1958, that I was advised by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources that the low rental housing scheme which I have described had reached the stage where tenders were to be called for the end of March, 1958, with construction to start early in May. The whole arrangement was, of course, subject to the Yukon legislative council giving the commissioner of the Yukon the necessary authority to enter into the appropriate agreements with the federal government and for the establishment of a housing authority. The council also had to authorize the territorial government to assume one quarter of the capital cost but it is important to know that that one-quarter of the capital cost of the project was to be borrowed by the territorial government from the federal government through the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. On the same day, namely, February 10, 1958, I was informed by the Minister of Public Works that a submission had been forwarded to the Yukon legislative council recommending the approval of an agreement regarding the low rental housing project pursuant to section 36 of the National Housing Act and section 18 of the Yukon Act, such project to be undertaken jointly by the commissioner of the Yukon and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Without going into the details of the project itself, it involved the expenditure of approximately $550,000 and would have made available 30 units which would have been rented to needy tenants at a rental of $70 per month. This included an element of subsidization of $35, the cost of which was to be borne in the same proportions as I have indicated, namely 75 per cent by the federal government and 25 per cent by the territorial government, the funds for the latter purpose to be borrowed from the federal government. It was at this time that the project began to deteriorate. It is my personal opinion, without intending to cast any aspersions upon the

National Housing Act
commissioner of the Yukon, because he cannot answer me here, that it began to deteriorate because of certain doubts expressed by him as to the feasibility of the project, certain doubts with respect to whether or not the units would be occupied completely and certain doubts as to the design of the project, doubts which at least contributed to the Yukon legislative council failing to approve the project.
There remains a very desperate need for low rental housing in the Yukon, particularly in Whitehorse. The plans are still available for this project and after recent consultations with officials of C.M.H.C. I have been advised that they are still prepared to give every consideration to the project. I assume that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) as well as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) would still be of the same view. Perhaps the Minister of Public Works would be prepared to give the municipality of Whitehorse that assurance when he closes the debate on second reading.
I should say that one of the main difficulties in building in the Yukon at all is the availability of funds to close the gap between the down payment necessary under C.M.H.C. and the down payment required under the act. One method by which this could be done, and which I suggested to the then minister of public works last session, is the institution of a second mortgage fund from which these moneys could be borrowed, a second mortgage fund which would be available not only to people outside the government service who wished to build but to federal civil servants who wished to buy or build their own homes. If such a fund had been available in past years the Liberal administration of the day would perhaps not have got into the difficulty where millions of dollars were expended on government housing which was somewhat ostentatious. I might also say that I have also spoken to many federal civil servants who have not only endorsed buying or building their own homes but have expressed themselves as very keenly in favour thereof.
I should like to conclude by remarks by once again requesting the minister to give me the assurance, either this evening or outside of the house or by correspondence, that the same approach is being taken by public works to the institution of a low rental housing scheme in Whitehorse and, indeed, in any municipality in the Yukon which displays a need for this type of housing. I should also say that a large amount of the blame, if indeed it can be called that, lies at the door of the two local governments concerned, 
namely, the municipal council and the territorial council of the day, in not pressing for the institution of a low rental housing scheme. I am not saying anything other than that I feel that if the two local governmental bodies were to make representations now to the minister or to C.M.H.C. for the necessary funds to implement this particular project or any modified version of it then the funds would be forthcoming. It is not a dead issue. It is an issue that is very much alive and I feel that the project can be brought into being simply by the municipal and territorial councils co-operating in a request to the government to implement the scheme in the city of Whitehorse and, indeed, the same thing can be done in any other municipality in the Yukon that can display a need for that type of housing.

We have been given the statistics on housing starts in Canada in recent years. In 1957, when this government took office, there were 122,340 housing starts; in 1958, this number had increased to 164,632. The government was fresh in office. It had new ideas. I will ask the minister, why the reduc-j tion? Why is less money available for homes? This I fail to understand. Is it because Canadians need fewer homes in 1960? Are we short of families to occupy the homes? Have we removed slum conditions in this country to the point where we can say we now have adequate housing and, therefore, we will cut back the program? speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: It is always a pleasure to hear the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) because, as we know, he is an authority on one subject, and that is wheat. Whenever he talks about anything else he merely creates a pattern of invective and rhetoric. He has not contributed to the debate-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
We are in a wonderful position tonight. We have in Canada today, as a result of this government coming into power, 400,000 new homes completed. Think of what that means. Think of all it means to the Canadian economy. Due to the winter works program of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker),
82.000	homes are being built. We have a greater volume of construction going on in the building of homes in Canada today than in almost any previous year in the history of the nation. The government has placed tens of thousands-hundreds of thousands- of people, in houses of their own, people who could never have dreamed of owning a modern home had this government not come into power.
We have in prospect this year the completion of the 82,000 homes which are in the process of being built. Now starts will include between 80,000 and 85,000 homes built with the aid of conventional loans in which the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation does not participate. We have, in addition,
20.000	homes, 20,000 starts, through approved lenders. With or without the participation of banks there may be 20,000 of these homes and, with the $150 million allocated by Central Mortgage for direct loans, another 15,000 and, in addition, a further 3,000 or 5,000 units under limited dividend housing. That is the

answer to the hon. member for Assiniboia, the authority on wheat. That is our answer on housing.
I have been asked about the interest rate. Everybody was satisfied with the interest rate at 6 J per cent until the opposition tried to stir up blue ruin. The hon. member for Assiniboia thinks it is too high. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) thinks it is too low. They are all mixed up. There are three leaders in that party at the present time, and after the contribution of the hon. member for Assiniboia tonight there will be two. I never heard such gross nonsense in my life. Is not the rate of 6J per cent attractive enough to bring the approved lenders into the market again? Where could they get a more attractive investment, considering that this a loan insured by the government at a time when they would only get 5-J per cent on government bonds? Is the hon. member suggesting that we should put it lower than that, and not get anything from the approved lenders? We are interested in the little man. We are getting the approved lenders back into the market as they were before, and we do not want their confidence to be broken down by snide, ignorant remarks from hon. members of the opposition of whom the hon. member for Assiniboia is the chief.
Was there any other question which the hon. member for Assiniboia asked in his rhetorical remarks to which he wants an answer before ten o'clock? If not, let me say this. So far tonight we have had no constructive suggestions from the C.C.F. group. On the other hand, we have received considerable assistance from the Liberal party, and I am surprised to be able to say that. So far the helpful suggestions from the Liberal group are that we should this year increase the frills; that we should carry out more urban redevelopment; that we should have the sewers paid for by the federal government; that we should cut out the insurance premium; that we should hold more design competitions, and so on.
What we are talking about is building homes for the ordinary man in as great a number as we can. That is what this government is engaged in, and we approach ten o'clock-I am only going to adjourn the debate until tomorrow afternoon-may I say this in closing: it is not possible to go on forever with this fantastic amount of building. We are delighted that it has gone on until now. We predict in this year 1960 an unprecedented year of prosperity. Hon. members have seen estimates showing that we expect there will be spent in Canada $8.7 billions on capital expenditure this year. How

can they expect us to keep up the same record as we have had in the last three years in housing?
Some of the suggestions we receive from the other side are incredible. Tomorrow I may perhaps be permitted to answer in detail many of the queries raised by the opposition, and I will try to be as brief as possible.
May I call it ten o'clock and adjourn the debate?

1.	How many applications were rceelved by the civil service commission at Montreal in connection with competition No. 59-1192, Dorval air terminal?
2.	After examination, did the examining board recommend certain persons to the civil service commission, Montreal, as being qualified to fill the position?

Answer by:	Hon. Leon Balcer (Acting
Secretary of Stale):
1.	Fifty applications were received by the civil service commission at Montreal in connection with competition No. 59-1192, superintendent, terminal building, Montreal airport.
2.	The examining board at Montreal recommended three candidates as qualified for the position.
3.	During consideration of the board's recommendation, the commission received reports on the top-ranking candidate from the commission's Montreal district office, the commission officer in charge of selection for the department, and the department itself. In the light of these reports, the commission was of the opinion that none of the candidates was fully qualified to fill the position in question. Accordingly the competition was cancelled and re-advertised on a new Canadawide basis under competition No. 60-489.
4.	The candidates were notified in writing that the competition had been cancelled and that their applications were being transferred to the new competition.
5.	No.
